1.4  Gold Nanoparticles

Biomedical Applicability

Like iron oxide, gold is a useful nanomaterial in medical applications with multiple
capabilities. Gold can serve as a platform for the attachment of various moieties.22 This is

11

[PDF page 12]
possible because ligands with polar functional groups such as thiols, phosphines, and amines,
spontaneously self-assemble on gold surfaces.22 In addition, gold is highly biocompatible and

inert, providing it with desirable qualities for use in biological systems.23 For additional

biocompatibility, gold is often coated with poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG).24 PEG has the repeat

OCH2CH2 subunit with terminal hydroxyl groups, making it extremely hydrophilic and
flexible.25 Therefore, PEG is a commonly used agent to increase the blood half-life and stability

of Au NP-based constructs.24 Furthermore, Au NPs can be decorated with various therapeutic

agents to target and destroy cancer cells. For example, methotrexate is a chemotherapeutic agent
capable of treating several cancer types.26 Chen et al. prepared a gold-methotrexate conjugate

nanoparticle for testing on mice.26 It was found that the conjugate system inhibited growth of

Lewis lung carcinoma tumors compared to the untreated control mice.26

Application: Thermal Ablation

Au NPs can also be used for thermal ablation therapy because of the surface plasmon
resonance phenomenon characteristic of Au NPs.27 When light hits Au NPs, the surface

plasmons or coherent electron oscillations on the surface are generated, imparting the
nanoparticles with unique optical properties.27 Compared to hyperthermia, thermal ablation

requires that cancer cells are heated to higher elevated temperatures, between 50–100°C.28 When

near-infrared light (NIR) impinges upon aggregates of Au NPs, the nanoparticles are strongly
heated through absorption of this radiation.29 NIR laser light is used for thermal ablation therapy

because hemoglobin and water have minimal absorption in this wavelength range.29 When NIR

light hits Au NPs, the surface plasmons become highly energized through electron-electron
collisions.30 The high energy electrons then interact with phonons, which is the vibrational

12

[PDF page 13]
oscillations of Au atoms in the Au NPs.30,31 The energy from these electron-phonon interactions

are then released to cause tumor cell death.29

Several groups have investigated thermal ablation with different Au NP systems. Hirsch

et al. used nanoparticle hybrids with a silica core and an external gold shell coated with PEG for
an in vitro study with human breast carcinoma cells.32 With exposure to NIR light for 7 minutes,

all cells revealed photothermal destruction. Gold nanorods can also be used for photothermal

therapy. In one study, PEGylated gold nanorods were administered to mice with subcutaneous
squamous cell carcinoma xenografts through direct and intraveneous injection.33 The mice were

then subject to NIR radiation for a duration of 10 minutes, immediately following direct

injection. Nanorods were allowed to circulate for twenty-four hours for mice that received the

therapy intravenously in order to allow for accumulation of the nanorods within the tumor. These

mice were also exposed to NIR for 10 minutes. Over thirteen days, researchers found inhibition

of tumor growth using both delivery methods.

1.5  Coupling Iron Oxide and Gold

Combining the imaging power of FexOy NPs with the surface functionalization abilities

and biocompatibility of gold nanomaterials through various conjugate systems has garnered
much research interest. Gold protects the iron oxide core against oxidation.8 As discussed

previously, it also provides functionality, making iron oxide-gold shell nanoparticle systems

desirable for biomedical applications. There are multiple designs to combine FexOy and Au NPs

together. To coat FexOy NPs with gold, researchers have employed different methods.

The simplest route is to directly coat bare FexOy NPs with gold. However, this is a

difficult process because bare FexOy NPs aggregate in solution forming large clusters of
nanoparticles.8 This hinders the ease of creating a gold shell because the nanoparticles will not be

13

[PDF page 14]
well-dispersed in solution for the deposition of the gold shell. Furthermore the two surfaces are
very different, resulting in minimal contact between the iron oxide and gold surfaces.34

A common method to create core-shell, iron oxide-gold complexes is to functionalize the

surface of FexOy NPs with other ligand stabilizers. 3-aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (APTMS) or

some other amine-terminated organosilane can be functionalized directly onto FexOy NPs. The

affinity of amines for gold can then be exploited by decorating the surface with small Au NPs.

Finally, a gold shell is formed by reduction of gold cations around the Au NPs in the presence of

a reducing agent. Levin et al. followed this procedure in creating gold-coated wüstite
nanoparticles.35 A solution of chloroauric acid and potassium carbonate was added to the

nanoparticles following attachment with 2 nm Au NPs, and upon the addition of formaldehyde as
the reducing agent, the gold shell formed.35

Another strategy is to create an intermediate layer on FexOy NPs to stabilize the

nanoparticles before formation of the gold shell. Coating iron oxide with silica provides a
number of distinct advantages. Silica is an extremely transparent, dielectric material.36 Since

silica cannot absorb visible or near IR light or conduct electricity, it is an ideal material for
combining iron oxide and gold because it does not compromise the properties of either.36 A silica

surface has surface silanol groups that can easily react with alcohols and silane coupling
agents.37 Coating FexOy NPs with silica stabilizes the nanoparticles in solution even in high

particle and electrolyte concentrations and over wide pH ranges.38 Finally, a silica layer

augments the biocompatibility of FexOy NPs because it is non-cytotoxic and also prevents FexOy
NPs from oxidizing.39

The most common method to create a silica coating is the Stӧber process. Several authors
have employed this method.40,41,42 The silica coating is formed through hydrolysis and

14

[PDF page 15]
condensation of silicon oxides, most commonly tetraethylorthosilicate (TEOS), with water and a
base such as ammonium hydroxide or ammonia in ethanol.43 In a typical procedure, TEOS is

added to a suspension of FexOy NPs in ethanol with a base and water, followed by stirring.41 The

thickness of the silica layer is controlled through the amount of TEOS added.41

Ji et al. used commercially available FexOy NPs thought to be coated with oleic acid,
which acts as a stabilizer.41 The mean diameter of the silica-coated FexOy NPs was 66.0 ± 9.5

nm. Maurice et al. prepared FexOy NPs grafted with citrate anions so that the NPs remained
stable in solution at physiological pH.42 Citrate anions assisted the coating process because

TEOS had increased affinity to the iron oxide surface. The mean diameter of the core-shell

nanoparticles ranged from 94 to 261 nm. Salgueiriño-Maceira et al. were able to coat bare FexOy
NPs with silica.40 The resulting nanoparticles, shown in a TEM image in Figure 6, had an

average diameter of 170 nm.

Several groups have modified the Stӧber process through a microemulsion method using

a water-in-oil microemulsion and a reverse microemulsion. For the water-in-oil microemulsion,

[PDF page 16]
there are three components, water, oil, which is an organic solvent, and a surfactant.44 Because of

its amphiphilicity, a surfactant molecule lowers the interfacial tension between water and oil so
that two liquids are miscible.44 Tiny droplets of water suspended in the bulk oil act as reaction

vessels to coat the nanoparticles with silica.44 The size of the nanoparticles is dependent on the

water droplet size, which can be modified by changing the water-to-surfactant molar ratio.44

Santra et al. investigated three different non-ionic surfactants—Triton X-100, Brij-97 and
Igepal CO-520, shown in Figure 7—for this technique.44 In a typical experiment, two

microemulsions were prepared. Microemulsion 1 (ME1) contained Fe2+ and Fe3+ salts in water

and the other, ME2, had either sodium hydroxide or ammonium hydroxide and TEOS in water,

while both contained surfactant dispersed in cyclohexane. ME2 was slowly added to ME1 to

form FexOy NPs coated with silica. Santra et al. were able to obtain silica layer thicknesses

between 1–2 nm.

1.6  Project Description and Goals

The primary goal of our project is to create a nanoparticle, shown schematically in Figure

8, capable of selectively targeting, imaging, and damaging pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

Figure 8. Idealized representation of fully assembled nanoparticle. Note all components are to scale.

Specifically, my focus is on creating the iron oxide-gold shell conjugate. The complete

nanoparticle contains an iron oxide core serving as a contrast agent for MR imaging. A gold shell

envelops the iron oxide core and is used as a platform for attaching different chemical moieties.

PEG terminated with a thiol group at one end and biotin at the other coats the gold surface for

17

[PDF page 18]
additional biocompatibility and for coupling with avidin. Avidin is a protein with four binding
sites and binds strongly with biotin.47 The chimeric human-mouse monoclonal antibody, CHO

31.1, which specifically targets the antigen A33 expressed in pancreatic tumor cells, binds to
avidin.48 Finally the biotinylated therapeutic agent, poly (D-glutamate: D-lysine) (poly-GL)

loaded with boron-10 occupies the remaining sites on avidin. Boronated poly-GL is used for

boron neutron capture therapy whereby after irradiation with thermal neutrons, high energy alpha
particles are produced and destroy tumor cells.49 Alpha particles have a limited path length of 5-9

µm and so are confined to cancerous cells that have internalized the NPs so that normal cells are
largely unaffected.49

My objectives are three-fold:

(1) synthesize iron oxide nanoparticles coated with gold (FexOy/Au NPs),

(2) chemically attach different moieties to the surface of FexOy/Au NPs by functionalization,

and

(3) characterize the properties and stability of FexOy/Au NPs after each modification.

Previously, Sherry Zhou and Hatice Yayla tested different methods to create the gold
shell using the coupling agent, APTMS, to act as binding sites for 2 nm Au NPs.50,51 Afterwards,

the gold shell was created with the addition of a gold salt and a reducing agent. Specifically,

Zhou and Yayla attempted the Levin synthesis by using potassium tetrachloroaurate and
potassium carbonate with hydroxylamine and hydrochloric acid, following seeding.35 A major

setback was the presence of uncoated FexOy NPs and difficulty in effectively removing them

from coated NPs. Zhou also tried creating the gold shell on FexOy NPs through iterative

hydroxylamine seeding according to the Lyon synthesis, however the NPs were greater than 50

nm and therefore not useful because the overall nanoparticle must be between 50–100 nm in

diameter.52 Building off of this work, I aim to create the gold shell through the synthetic scheme

outlined in Figure 9 with Gold Enhance™.

2.3  Synthetic Methods

FexOy NPs (Kang NPs) Synthesis
Kang NPs were synthesized using a co-precipitation method developed by Kang et al.53

FeCl2•4H2O (0.8 g) and FeCl3•6H2O (2.08 g) were dissolved in a 1:2 mole ratio in a

deoxygenated solution of HCl (340 µL, 12.1 N) and nH2O (10 mL) and the solution was again

purged with nitrogen gas for another 10 minutes. The solution was then well-sealed with two

strips of parafilm to limit opportunistic oxygen. This clear yellow-orange iron chloride solution

was then added drop-wise over 8 minutes to a deoxygenated solution of NaOH (100 mL, 1.5 M)

previously purged for 30 minutes. To do this, the alkaline solution was set to a vigorous stir with

a magnetic stir bar and nitrogen gas pressure was maintained in the system while the iron

chloride solution was added. Black particles formed almost instantly and after addition of the

iron chloride solution was complete, the resulting solution was black. Kang NPs were collected

overnight using a magnet (Qiagen Cat # 36910) and the supernatant was pipetted out. The

product was washed and collected 3 times with 150 mL of deoxygenated nH2O for each wash.

Finally, the product was washed with HCl (200 mL, 0.01 M) and then resuspended in nH2O. If

air is present during the synthesis, maghemite, γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles form resulting in a rusty-
brown product.53 UV-vis spectroscopy, DLS, and TEM studies were done to characterize the

colloid.

3  Results and Discussion

3.1  Synthesis and Characterization of FexOy NPs

Creating FexOy/Au NPs couples the imaging capability of SPIOs with the surface

functionality and desirable biomedical properties of gold. An iron oxide core of approximately

10 nm in diameter is needed to satisfy the 50–100 nm size requirement of the fully functionalized

nanoparticle. The 50–100 nm size range for the complete nanoparticle was determined by studies
examining the distribution of spherical gold nanoparticles of different sizes in the body.56,57,58

Two crucial criteria were found. Nanoparticles must be of a size sufficiently large to selectively

enter target organs and small enough to evade the body’s immune defenses. We investigated two

types of magnetite, FexOy NPs for the creation of FexOy/Au NPs, synthesized Kang NPs and

commercially available Ferrotec NPs.

Kang NPs
Kang NPs were synthesized using a facile co-precipitation technique with Fe2+ and Fe3+

ions in basic conditions yielding spherical, magnetite, Fe3O4 NPs with a reported value of 8.5 ±
1.3 nm.53 Alternative methods to create FexOy NPs are possible but require difficult conditions

such as thermal decomposition of an iron precursor in organic solvents.59 This co-precipitation

technique was chosen for its simplicity and because it fit the size condition. This synthesis

produces FexOy NPs of a suitable size so that with the addition of subsequent components to the

magnetic core, the final nanoparticle is within the size limit of 50–100 nm. The product was

investigated through UV-vis spectroscopy, DLS, and TEM.

The UV-vis absorption spectrum of bare Kang NPs is shown in Figure 10. Kang NPs did

not possess a characteristic peak between 200–800 nm, but exhibited increasing absorbance

starting from 800 nm. In a study of magnetite nanoparticles, which appear black, nanoparticles

produced through the Kang synthesis displayed increasing absorbance in the 800–400 nm

27

[PDF page 28]
spectral range, with a minimum at approximately 800 nm.60 The absorption spectrum of Kang

NPs presented in Figure 10 agrees with this study and suggests successful creation of Kang NPs.

Figure 10. UV-vis absorption spectrum of Kang NPs suspended in nanopure water.

DLS is a useful characterization technique because it analyzes the size and size

distribution of particles in solution. Specifically, DLS provides the hydrodynamic diameter, or

size and the polydispersity index (PDI), or the relative size distribution of the nanoparticles in

solution on a scale of 0 to 1, with 1 as the most polydisperse. DLS measurements of Kang NPs

suspended in ethanol yielded a hydrodynamic diameter of 266.8 nm and a PDI of 0.18 even after

sonication to homogenize the colloidal solution, and filtration to remove material larger than 450

nm. This measured value is far larger than the expected value of 8.5 nm and is likely a result of

individual nanoparticles aggregating together because of their strong magnetic dipoles to form

large clusters. A PDI of 0.18 suggests that the nanoparticle clusters are of fairly uniform size.

The Kang synthesis produces bare magnetite nanoparticles and as noted before in Section 1.3,

magnetite nanoparticles need to be modified with a stabilizing ligand to avoid aggregation.

3.2  Functionalization of FexOy NPs with APTMS

In the first step for the formation of

FexOy/Au NPs, FexOy NPs must be functionalized

with APTMS. This small organic molecule
promotes adsorption of 2 nm Au NPs to the surface  Figure 14. Chemical structure of APTMS.

of FexOy NPs. APTMS, shown in Figure 14, has a silicon atom bonded to three methoxy groups

and an amine-terminated propyl group. Organosilanes like APTMS are frequently used as

linking agents to modify the surface of both iron oxide and silica nanoparticles for the

preliminary evaluation.

Although FT-IR can demonstrate that FexOy NPs are functionalized with APTMS, it

Maximizing APTMS coverage is an important goal because a highly amine-terminated surface

should theoretically increase the number of 2 nm Au NPs studding the nanoparticles, which in

an amine assay. An amine assay entails reacting the terminal amine groups in APTMS with a

selective fluorophore, which forms a nanoparticle-fluorophore complex that produces a strong

fluorescence signal. The intensity of the fluorescence signal is then dependent on the number of

primary amines on the metal oxide surface.

3.3  Seeding of Ferrotec with 2 nm Au NPs

After creating the amine-terminated surface on FexOy NPs, 2 nm Au NPs are used as

nucleation sites for the formation of a continuous gold shell around the magnetic core. 2 nm Au
NPs direct growth of the gold shell in the presence of a gold salt and a reducing agent.54 Islands

of gold form around the 2 nm Au NPs and eventually coalesce to create a continous gold shell.54

Uptake of the Au NPs was attempted with UV-vis spectroscopy. However, the results proved

inconsistent from batch to batch and within batches of seeded Ferrotec NPs. For results and

discussion of this portion, see appendix, section 5.1. Seeded Ferrotec NPs were not analyzed

through transmission electron microscopy because observing the 2 nm Au NPs is beyond the

resolution capabilities of the TEM instrument.

3.4  Formation of Gold Shell

Once FexOy NPs are functionalized with APTMS and decorated with 2 nm Au NPs, the

final step is to reduce gold cations clustered around the Au NPs to create the gold shell. Gold

Enhance™ is the gold coating kit and contains four components designated A through D.

According to the Nanoprobes website, A is the enhancer, B is the activator, C is the initiator, and
D is the buffer and each component must be added in equal volume for gold shell growth.68 The

precise identity of each component is proprietary information. Gold Enhance™ is a kit

specifically designed to grow gold shells on gold nanoparticles for study using light microscopy.

Therefore, we did a test run of the gold coating on precursor Kang and Ferrotec NPs deposited

on TEM grids; results and discussion are presented in the appendix, section 5.2.

Gold Coating of Ferrotec NPs in Solution

Creating gold shells on individual FexOy NPs requires that the nanoparticles are highly

stable in solution. If FexOy NPs are clustered together during the coating process then groups of

FexOy NPs will be encased in gold, rather than individual nanoparticles. Thus, we focused on

Ferrotec NPs for the creation of the gold shell because Ferrotec NPs were significantly more

stable in nanopure water than Kang NPs, as detailed in Section 3.1, displaying less aggregation

problems. The importance of restricting the final nanoparticle conjugate between 50–100 nm in

diameter to ensure its effectiveness in vivo, necessitates a thin gold shell.

A preliminary study was conducted to obtain an estimate of the volume of Gold

Enhance™ (GE) needed to form the gold shell on seeded Ferrotec NPs. Ferrotec NPs

functionalized with 0.5 µL of APTMS and attached to 2 nm Au NPs were coated with various

volumes (8, 40, 200, or 1000 µL) of GE.

39

[PDF page 40]
UV-vis spectroscopy is the primary initial screening method to determine if a gold shell

forms on FexOy NPs. Once FexOy NPs are enclosed in gold, the surface plasmon resonance

phenomenon of gold can be observed. Three important characteristics of the plasmon band

provide useful information about FexOy/Au NPs, its position, bandwidth, which is measured by

the full width at half of the maximum absorbance (FWHM), and baseline. The shell thickness

and extent of nanoparticle aggregation influence these three characteristics.

Overall, once the gold shell is formed, a strong absorbance maximum ranging from 500-
700 nm should result.35,52,54 In the synthesis of gold-coated wüstite nanoparticles, Levin et al.

observed that as the shell thickness increased from 11 to 45 nm, the surface plasmon peak
starting at approximately 600 nm shifted to longer wavelengths.35 Furthermore, as the gold shell

increased in thickness, the bandwidth of the surface plasmon band increased as well.35 However,

aggregation is also another factor confounding peak position and contributes to peak width. Lyon

et al. created gold-coated maghemite nanoparticles with 9 nm size cores through an iterative

process whereby gold cations were repeatedly reduced on the iron oxide surface with
hydroxylamine hydrochloride as the reducing agent.52 Interestingly, they found with increasing

iterations of the coating step, the average diameters of the nanoparticles decreased from 62 nm to

59 and 57 nm with 1, 3, and 5 iterations. The shell thickness decreased because a fuller shell

formed, making the nanoparticles more uniform and smaller in size and spherical with each

iteration. Furthermore, inspection of TEM images of coated nanoparticles with 1, 3, and 5

iterations suggest that with more iterations, the nanoparticles aggregated less. Agreeing with

findings from the Levin synthesis, the absorption spectra with 1, 3, and 5 iterations show that as

the gold shell thickness decreased the surface plasmon band shifted from approximately 600 nm

to 540 nm and the width of the bands decreased. With aggregation, the bandwidth of the surface

40

[PDF page 41]
plasmon band also increased. Finally, Xi and coworkers created FexOy/Au NPs with an
intermediate silica layer.41 They observed with increasing shell growth, higher absorbance of the

surface plasmon baseline, indicating aggregation of the nanoparticles.

Figure 18 shows UV-vis spectra of a preliminary attempt using various volumes of Gold

Enhance™ (GE) on seeded precursor Ferrotec NPs. With 200 µL of GE, the surface plasmon

band had a peak absorbance at 566 nm whereas with 1000 µL of GE, the band had a maximum at

657 nm. From the presence of absorption bands in the 500-700 nm region, we can deduce the

presence of gold with 200 and 1000 µL of GE. Furthermore, 200 µL of GE resulted in an

absorption maximum at a shorter wavelength compared to 1000 µL of GE, indicating the

formation of a thinner gold shell. No absorbance characteristic of gold is present for 8 and 40 µL

of GE. Additionally, there is a distinct difference in the broadness of the two peaks. With 1000

µL, the width of the peak is very broad, stretching from nearly 800–500 nm and the FWHM

cannot be calculated, whereas with 200 µL, the absorbance band is much narrower with a

FWHM of 222 nm. Finally, considering the baselines of the two bands, at 800 nm the plasmon

band has a baseline of 0.25 and 0.12 for the 1000 and 200 µL samples, respectively and there is

high absorption across the entire spectral window with these two samples. Visual inspection of

the 200 µL and 1000 µL samples found that the samples appeared cloudy, suggesting there was

scattering because of large nanoparticles. The 200 µL sample was purple and fairly clear and the

1000 µL sample was light-pink in color and cloudy. Considering the 1000 µL sample,

absorbance at higher wavelengths and a broad absorption band suggest the nanoparticles are

large and also were likely aggregating. With 200 µL, nanoparticles aggregated less and were

likely smaller.

Refinement of the Gold Coating Procedure

Reproducibility of the results with gold shell formation from the preliminary attempt was

poor. In the preliminary trial, the seeded Ferrotec NPs were not sonicated prior to deposition of

the gold shell. As described previously, FexOy nanoparticles must be stable and well

homogenized in solution to create a shell on individual nanoparticles. In attempts to reproduce

Ferrotec/Au NPs created with 200 µL of GE and to tune the thickness down by decreasing the

volume of GE added, the resulting products were of poor quality. With sonication prior to the

coating, the UV-vis spectra of the products were comparable to the UV-vis spectrum of

Ferrotec/Au NPs formed with 1000 µL of GE from the preliminary attempt. It was hypothesized

sonication may affect the weak chemical binding interactions between the terminal amine groups

of APTMS and the 2 nm Au NPs, because a significant amount of energy is imparted to the

nanoparticles in this process.

With this in mind, we explored different parameters in the overall synthesis of FexOy/Au

NPs to refine the process. In this trial, three parameters were adjusted, the volume of APTMS

46

[PDF page 47]
used for the functionalization step, sonication prior to the coating step, and the volume of GE.

The two different volumes of APTMS were chosen to determine the appropriate volume of

APTMS for optimum shell formation. As explained in section 3.2, a highly amine-terminated

surface is postulated to be valuable for maximizing the number of 2 nm Au NPs attached to the

nanoparticle, which dictates the success of forming the gold shell. In addition to sonication, the

amount of GE was varied to decrease the gold shell thickness from approximately 20-35 nm in

diameter, as reported in the first attempt, to obtain a thinner shell. Exacerbating the challenge of

working with these samples, a considerable number of nanoparticles were lost in wash steps after

the coating, making further characterization difficult because of limited sample. The volume of

seeded Ferrotec NPs and GE used for the coating was scaled up by five, compared to the

preliminary attempt detailed above.

The different parameters in this attempt were 0.5 µL and 10 µL of APTMS, 200 µL and

160 µL equivalents of GE (relative to the preliminary trial) and half of the samples were

sonicated while the remainder was not. Considering the three adjustable parameters, a total of

eight samples were produced. All 8 samples were analyzed through UV-vis spectroscopy and

from them the most promising samples were analyzed with TEM. In presenting the UV-vis

spectra, for brevity and clarity, spectra of the most representative samples illustrating the effect

of each parameter are presented and discussed below. For reference, in all UV-vis spectra, YS

means yes sonication and NS means no sonication.

Figure 22 presents an overlay of two UV-vis spectra for two different samples of

Ferrotec/Au NPs previously functionalized with 0.5 µL (black) and 10 µL of APTMS (red), with

all other parameters kept constant. The absorbance maxima were 558 nm (FWHM=226 nm) and

543 nm (FWHM=152 nm) for 0.5 and 10 µL of APTMS, respectively. Findings from other

47

[PDF page 48]

a plasmon band shifted to shorter wavelengths and possessing a smaller bandwidth. From the

peak positions and bandwidths of the two samples, with 10 µL of APTMS, a thinner gold shell

was likely formed. This finding applied to all pairs of samples where the only difference was the

volume of APTMS. Furthermore, the color of Ferrotec/Au NPs formed with 0.5 µL of APTMS

was an intermediate color between pink and purple, whereas with 10 µL of APTMS, the sample

appeared purple. From the preliminary attempt at creating Ferrotec/Au NPs in solution,

Ferrotec/Au NPs of a smaller size appeared purple. Both samples had high absorption across the

entire spectral range and the samples appeared slightly cloudy. This is likely because of

scattering as a result of large nanoparticles and possibly aggregation of the nanoparticles. From

these results, a high volume of APTMS is useful to seeding Ferrotec NPs to increase the number

of 2 nm Au NPs on the surface of the nanoparticles so that a thinner gold shell is formed.

Ferrotec NPs, sonication is important to producing a thin gold shell. However, further studies

should be done to determine if the contradictory results shown with different volumes of APTMS

4  Conclusions and Future Directions

Significant efforts were made towards the creation of the FexOy/Au NP to be incorporated

in the fully functionalized nanoparticle targeting pancreatic cancer. Two types of FexOy NPs

55

[PDF page 56]
were tested towards the creation of the complete nanoparticle. A co-precipitation method was

used to synthesize 8-10 nm Kang NPs, yet the instability of Kang NPs in solution limited their

use in the creation of FexOy/Au NPs. Commercially available Ferrotec NPs proved to be more

stable from DLS measurements and visual observations.

The steps leading to the creation of the gold shell on FexOy NPs were analyzed to obtain a

better understanding of the process. IR spectroscopy and an amine assay proved useful analytical

tools to determine functionalization of FexOy NPs with APTMS and to optimize this step for the

subsequent attachment of 2 nm Au NPs. Uptake of 2 nm Au NPs proved inconclusive through

UV-vis spectroscopy and encourages further study. Attempts at controlling the gold shell

thickness and investigating the impact of three parameters involved in the gold coating process

revealed three preliminary findings. Maximizing APTMS surface coverage for optimal

attachment of 2 nm Au NPs, sonication of seeded NPs, and limiting the volume of Gold

Enhance™ are important to create FexOy/Au NPs of small and monodisperse size. To observe

contrast of FexOy NPs upon various modifications during the coating process, a qualitative study

of seeded and gold-coated Ferrotec NPs revealed detectable negative contrast.

Several problems were also experienced at various stages in the creation of FexOy/Au

NPs. Kang NPs were found to aggregate greatly and work should be done to stabilize them in

solution. To optimize the functionalization step for the attachment of 2 nm Au NPs, two further

suggestions ought to be pursued. Refluxing upon addition of APTMS to a suspension of FexOy

NPs should improve the formation of new silicon-oxygen bonds. The application of heat will

augment the formation of extensive polysiloxane networks, creating a high surface density of
terminal amines.63 In tandem with this additional experimental step, further amine assay studies

must be conducted to determine the maximum volume of APTMS to saturate the nanoparticle

56

[PDF page 57]
surface. Optimizing this step is likely to be crucial for the attachment of 2 nm Au NPs on FexOy

NPs, which then impacts gold shell formation. Further studies are encouraged to quantify uptake

of 2 nm Au NPs following functionalization. ICP analysis of seeded NPs with different volumes

of APTMS can provide a sense of 2 nm Au NP uptake. The issue of uncoated FexOy NPs,

following the gold coating must be resolved. Previous attempts to remove uncoated FexOy NPs
with acid were not successful as detailed in the thesis work of Hatice Yayla and Sherry Zhou.51,50

Immediate next steps include refining the coating step with Gold Enhance™ to determine

optimal conditions for the deposition of a thin gold shell. A thin gold shell is necessary to restrict

the size of the complete nanoparticle for its effectiveness in vivo. After removing uncoated FexOy

NPs, the next step would be to continue relaxivity studies of FexOy/Au NPs to quantify contrast.

Furthermore, FexOy/Au NPs should be tested with the developed surface chemistry on 11.2 nm

Au NPs towards the creation of the complete nanoparticle.

5  Appendix

5.1  Uptake of 2 nm Au NPs

Colloidal gold nanoparticles exhibit surface plasmon resonance (SPR).27 SPR is a

phenomenon that occurs when plasmons on the surface of Au NPs interact with light, resulting in

intense absorption signals or plasmon bands when Au NPs are studied through UV-vis
spectroscopy.27 The characteristics of the plasmon band, like the absorbance maximum and

bandwidth depend on the size, shape, dielectric constant, and extent of aggregation of the
nanoparticles.70 Au NPs measuring 11.2 nm in diameter are wine-red in color, absorb at 518 nm,

and possess a sharp plasmon band.71 The absorbance maximum shifts to shorter wavelengths

(“blue shifts”) as the nanoparticle diameter decreases and the plasmon band broadens and

57

[PDF page 58]
decreases in intensity.23 Au NPs that are 2 nm in diameter are colorless and absorb in the

ultraviolet region.72 It was found experimentally that 2 nm Au NPs absorb in the ultraviolet

region at 187 nm, with a smaller absorption band at 220 nm. Furthermore, the UV-vis absorption

spectrum of FexOy in the ultraviolet region contains several intense peaks, masking the signals

from 2 nm Au NPs.

The overlap of intense plasmon bands for FexOy NPs with the optical signature for the Au

seeds required that we determine Au NP uptake indirectly. To do this the supernatant, or the

remaining liquid containing free Au NPs after collection of FexOy NPs with a magnet following

the seeding step, was analyzed. Compared to the absorbance maximum of pure Au NPs, the

supernatant should display a smaller absorbance because fewer Au NPs are present. However,

this change in absorbance was not consistent within batches and after seeding Ferrotec NPs

functionalized with different volumes of APTMS.

Figure 26 shows representative UV-vis spectra of 2 nm Au NPs, supernatants of Ferrotec

NPs functionalized with 0.5 µL and 10 µL of APTMS, and a negative control consisting of bare

Ferrotec NPs. The absorbance intensities at 187 nm are 1.95, 1.09, and 1.02 for 2 nm Au NPs,

0.5 and 10 µL of APTMS, respectively. The absorbance values for functionalized nanoparticle

have decreased, suggesting uptake of 2 nm Au NPs. However, the absolute absorbance values

cannot be trusted because these values are not consistent. Within this same batch the absorbance

values were 1.00, 1.09, 1.20, and 1.19 with seeded Ferrotec NPs functionalized with 0.5 µL of

APTMS. Additionally with 10 µL of APTMS seeded Ferrotec NPs had absorbance values of

1.12, 0.968, 1.22 and 1.02. Therefore it was not possible to theoretically quantify the number of

Au NPs on Ferrotec NPs following seeding. Examining the control (green spectrum) contrary to

expectations, the control also showed uptake. This could result from weak electrostatic

58

[PDF page 59]
interactions between Ferrotec NPs, which are coated with an unidentified stabilizer, and 2 nm Au

NPs, presumably capped with a negatively charge capping agent.

digested to determine the concentrations of gold and iron through ICP-OES.

# Lord Wellesley's confrontation with the Maratha 'Empire'

Author
*    Halliwell, William Arthur Clare [![Image 1: ISNI](https://ethos.bl.uk/assets/isni-d7693fcd6f049102061e6e7018c466c2978107873741f324ca0ce7c7baf80a31.png)](http://www.isni.org/isni/0000000135278377)

Qualification Name
*   Thesis (Ph.D.)

University
*   University of Southampton

Date Awarded
*   1999

[Access thesis from university](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/42326/)  

 Restricted 

- [x] 
The purpose of the thesis is to reinterpret Lord Wellesley's forward policy in India, with particular reference to his dealings with the Marathas, and to consider its motivation and the reasons for its failure. Lord Wellesley was the product of his age and environment. He was a colonial with ambitions to play a major role in metropolitan affairs. At the time of his appointment as Governor General of India the most important aspect of metropolitan concerns was the war with France, so that a major element in his policy was the protection of India from French interference. His policy was formed before he reached India, and had as its motivation, not only fear of the French, but fear of aggression by the Indian rulers, with or without French support. This fear derived from a conviction that Indian rulers were totally untrustworthy; only treaties permitting British control of their affairs (subsidiary treaties) could be effective to preserve peace in India. A balance of power between the Indian states, which was thought to have existed five years earlier, had been destroyed. Lord Wellesley succeeded at Mysore and Hyderabad, but failed with the Marathas. His primary target had been the Pune state, which was emphasised in the autumn of 1800 by conditional orders given to Arthur Wellesley to occupy Pune in certain circumstances. These did not occur and he retired. Meanwhile a new treaty had been concluded with the Nizam which was intensely provocative to the Marathas. It involved the British in protecting the Nizam's territory from all comers, including the Marathas who had legitimate claims on the Nizam. Their pursuit of them was liable to lead to war at some point and the British obligation made Lord Wellesley's forward policy towards them irreversible. The Peshwa of Pune was driven from Pune by Holkar and concluded the Treaty of Bassein with the British. This further provocation of the Marathas led to war with Sindhia and the Raja of Berar. The war was short lived and peace treaties were concluded with the Maratha chiefs separately by Arthur Wellesley who had been granted plenipotentiary powers in Western India. His policy was one of conciliation, not as Lord Wellesley's conquest. As a result the British failed to dominate Sindhia. Holkar now arrived on the scene and after abortive diplomatic exchanges war was declared on him. Lake the Commander-in-Chief failed to conquer Holkar, and Arthur Wellesley took no direct part in the war. Sindhia was sympathetic to Holkar and elements of his army, and, later, Sindhia himself, joined him. Lake's failure and Arthur Wellesley's divergent policy led to Lord Wellesley's failure to dominate the Marathas and, therefore, his failure to bring peace to India by conquest.

Holkar now arrived on the scene and after abortive diplomatic exchanges war was declared on him. Lake the Commander-in-Chief failed to conquer Holkar, and Arthur Wellesley took no direct part in the war. Sindhia was sympathetic to Holkar and elements of his army, and, later, Sindhia himself, joined him. Lake's failure and Arthur Wellesley's divergent policy led to Lord Wellesley's failure to dominate the Marathas and, therefore, his failure to bring peace to India by conquest.

Abstract:
Towards a Global Ethics:  The Debate on Nanotechnology in
the European Union and China

The primary aim of the thesis is to assess whether ethical governance of Science
and Technology is feasible as a global approach, using the example of
nanotechnology.
The thesis firstly compares ethical issues identified by stakeholders in China
and the EU relating to the rapid introduction of a potentially transformative
technology, namely nanotechnology.  Part One of this thesis explores how the
‘narratives’ of nanotechnology differ in each region, particularly given their different
bioethics contexts, and examines how specific concerns translate into policymaking.
In questioning whether Eastern and Western approaches to nanotechnology
governance can be aligned, one can observe that Europe is increasingly co-
operating and competing with China.  Such new interdependences between global
actors require new global approaches to S&T policy, including ethical governance.
Part Two of this thesis explores the concept of ‘global ethics’ and discusses
the feasibility of a global approach.  Given criticism of both universalism and
relativism, it is often argued that a universal approach that takes sufficient account of
local context cannot be developed.
On the assumption that global ethics are achieved by global actors, this
thesis looks at global agency.
The thesis connects discourse ethics and participatory Technology
Assessment (pTA), arguing that a version of Habermasian discourse ethics can
provide a theoretical framework for dialogue between West and East. Discourse
ethics has developed around Habermas’s argument that social order depends on our
capacity to recognize, through rational discourse, the intersubjective validity of
different views.  Habermas asks the basic question of global ethics, of how different
views (particularly of social order) can be universally recognized and agreed,
perhaps within an 'ideal community' of communication, one that may be global.
The thesis adds to Habermas’s discourse model, utilising virtue ethics as well
as the work of, for example, Taylor, Beck, Korsgaard and others on identity

ii

[PDF page 4]
formation.  It is argued that the significant factor in global ethics is the formation of
the agent’s moral identity, the formation of which requires one to go beyond one’s
context, to achieve an intercultural personhood.  Habermas (as do Taylor, Beck and
others) suggests identity as a dual concept, reflecting an interdependence of society
and one’s inner self.  This would mean that one can understand the cultural biases
inherent in any act of communication, while acting autonomously of such bias.
If such a model of dual identity/agency can be applied to the intercultural
dialogue on the governance of nanotechnology between East and West, it could
potentially provide a new tool or model within pTA.

Introduction: Towards a Global Ethics?  Science &
Technology Policy for Nanotechnology

Now nanotechnology had made nearly anything possible, and so the cultural role in
deciding what should be done with it had become far more important than imagining
what could be done with it.1

Our stubborn egocentricities lead us to believe that the world must be run according
to our own templates; that all would be well with the world if only it were populated
with people like us.  But our dehumanised apprehension of the familiar points directly
to the resolution.  Only when we come to understand, or even just acknowledge,
each other’s complexities can comprehension begin.  Only when we apprehend each
other as human...will the world begin to make sense.2

Nanotechnology has been described as equivalent to the development that kick-started
the industrial revolution;3 as a potential road to salvation for developing counties dealing

with issues of energy production, agricultural productivity enhancement, and water
treatment;4 but also as a Faustian bargain that may yet lead to global destruction.5

Although at present nanotechnology is used in a variety of products, ranging from skin
creams and food packaging to longer-lasting tennis balls and warmer socks, its potential is
as yet undefined (solar power for all!  A cure for cancer! Nanobots!), leading to both
utopian hype and dystopian dread.  Is it a form of miraculous engineering, a universal
nostrum, or a terrifyingly vague science that may ultimately reduce the universe to ‘grey

The facts are that nanotechnology will affect our lives (as indeed it already does
through products available on the market), and that surveys show it to be poorly
understood by the public in terms of its risks and benefits.8

An emerging science, nanotechnology provides an opportunity for the public to
work alongside researchers, corporations, and governments to attempt ethical
implementation.  It provides a test case for how the world might act given a technology that
could conceivably transform the global economy and provide solutions to major global
issues such as pollution, while potentially creating new environmental and health risks.
Nanotechnology, in particular, has been presented as a key site for experimenting with
novel forms of so-called upstream engagement, or efforts to engage members of the
public in dialogue about emerging technologies.9  It provides a context for the emergence

of a new risk governance paradigm, in terms of which local societies' political cultures and
risk perceptions become significant factors in risk assessment and governance, with
conventional top-down/authoritative decision-making models now taking more notice of
public risk discourse.10

How might the world act together to inculcate ethical concerns into nanopolicy as it is
formulated across the globe?  This broad question may seem both idealistic and futile, yet
it is only a restatement of a much older question about how to ensure that new
technologies affect us only with our consent.

This question raises several others:
(1) What are the particular and/or new ethical concerns that might be raised by a
new technology such as nano?
(2) How do we work together globally to agree on such concerns?
(3) And who is ‘we’? What skills and processes are required for such global
participation?

Given these 3 questions, encompassing a discussion of nanoethical issues, another of
global cooperation, and also of ‘skills and processes’, it is useful to be clearer regarding
the intent of this thesis. The study contributes, firstly, to a comparative understanding of
the environments within which nanotechnology is ‘regulated’ and discussed within China
and the EU.  Part I of this thesis (Chapter 1-3) thus offers a case study of (dis)similarity.
Part II of the thesis (Chapters 4-6) looks at how global ethics (given these differences)
might work, offering a proceduralist model, one of pTA (participatory Technology
Assessment).
The primary aim of this thesis is to provide an expanded pTA model, given my
premise that global ethics is best done through global agents in pTA. Habermasian
thought allows the expansion of current pTA models to predicate how agents might
achieve consensus – perhaps even global consensus (as Habermas’s ‘universalisation
principle’ suggests).
Nanotechnology as a globally significant new technology provides a useful case
study against which to examine how pTA (nanofora, for example) might work within and
across differing cultures such as those of the EU and China. Given nanotechnology's
significance in both regions as central to economic growth, agreement on the ethical
impact on society of such a potentially radical new technology would seem to be of
considerable importance.

1.  New concerns?
The first question is a very broad one, encompassing issues of military usage, distributive
justice (given that nanotechnology could have vast application in developing countries),
and risk management of toxicity, as well as more futuristic scenarios to do with human
enhancement.  No wonder that the range of potential nanotechnology applications has led
to debates about public involvement in decision-making.

Science journalist Philip Ball succinctly stated the problem in his article on why 2003
was ‘the year that society (in the UK that is) woke up to nanotechnology and got very
alarmed’.  Following the publication of Michael Crichton’s Prey in late 2002, and the start
of public debates in the UK media on the dangers of nanotechnology, Ball suggested the
following ethical questions should be asked:
Is nanotechnology primarily about wealth creation, or improving our quality of life, or
something else? Who is developing it, and why? With what responsibility, justification
and accountability? Who deals with potential problems, and how? Is there, and
should there be, a public mandate for it? The scientific community has no excuse for
ignoring such questions.11

Ethics and socio-ethical analysis have increasingly become an integral part of the
assessment of any new technology and its applications.12  Some countries, for example

the Netherlands, have instigated national programs dedicated to ethics in Science and
Technology (S&T) or have established academic institutes to conduct research into the

ethical implications of new technologies.  In China, ethical, legal and social implications
(ELSI) analysis is becoming a standard for evaluating new S&T developments.

Global variation in ELSI approaches to S&T development is however rather too large a
topic to be useful; this thesis attempts to narrow down the notion of ‘global’, by ‘West’
referring chiefly to the EU, and by ‘East’, principally to China.
Whereas the EU has a history of attempting communal social policy across its
member states (currently 27, with another 7 in candidature), the East has tended to form
economic policy clusters, although the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN
(currently 10 members), which also looks at social policy, can be noted.  There is no
common approach towards an Asian policy on nanotechnology, as there is in the EU, and
China has thus been selected for two reasons.  China is one of the two largest Eastern
‘players’ in nanotechnology S&T (the other being Japan).  China offers an interesting
example of a country that fully perceives the benefits of a new technology, including its

Part One of the thesis (Chapters 1-3) thus offers some comparative analysis of the

examines the EU and China to see if similar ethical issues relating to nanotechnology
development can be distinguished, or whether the ‘narratives’ of nanotechnology differ
markedly in each region, particularly given their bioethics contexts, which will be discussed
in Chapter Two.  Regional policies and regulations are then compared in Chapter Three.

In looking at a ‘global’ approach, the aim has been to select two regions that espouse
apparently diametric cultural values, such as Western individualism and so-called Eastern
communitarianism.  China is often regarded as the country that most clearly epitomises
so-called ‘Asian values’.  By Asian, ‘Confucian’ is usually meant, with a 'Confucian'
commitment to 'hard work, thrift, filial, piety and national pride' having encouraged rapid
economic growth in much of Asia.16  Amartya Sen, while suggesting the limitations of such

a generalisation, i.e. that it would be ‘a mistake both to see Confucianism as the only
tradition in Asia’ and to see Confucius as simply an authoritarian figure, notes however
that a Confucian authoritarian image is often taken as synonymous with ‘Asia’.17

Rather than the contentious term ‘Asian values’, however, which would for example not
have too much applicability to India,  perhaps ‘Orientalism’ is a more useful term, in that it
implies not so much  specific values, as a structure of antithesis.  Edward Said’s well-
known work on Orientalism suggests a dichotomy between ‘us and them’ exposed by
Western views of the East as inferior.  The dichotomy is central to both regions, whose
self-identification rests partly on definition through opposition – the East is ‘what the West
is not’, and vice versa.18  The social and cultural values underpinning bioethics debates in

China and the EU might suggest that it is a problem created by different ideas of one’s
social identity.  In the West, identity is driven by human rights discourses and the priority of
autonomy, whereas in the East, tao (harmony) and ren (benevolence) appear more highly
valued.
‘Otherness’ is an integral part of Said’s theories of how the clash of civilizations, of
East and West, has evolved through negation rather than recognition and acceptance of
the other’s differences.
China, for the purposes of this thesis, is posited as potentially, in its
communitarianism, antithetical to the EU, a useful ‘other’.
In the second half of this thesis, ‘otherness’ is explored in terms of collaborative or
dialogue structures that enable recognition.

2.  Global cooperation?
Is global consensus really necessary?  New interdependencies in S&T development, along
with a globalised and increasingly mobile market for S&T products, require some
agreement on how these technologies should be governed.
Global bodies have achieved some progress in addressing concerns about
nanotechnology.  These organisations include the International Council on Risk
Governance (IRGC), the International Council on Nanotechnology (ICON), the Globally

Harmonised Scheme for classification and labelling of substances (GHS), the International
Standards Organization (ISO), the Commission on the Ethics of Scientific Knowledge and
Technology (UNESCO/COMEST), the OECD Working Party on Nanotechnology (WPN),
and the OECD Working Party on Manufactured Nanomaterials (WPMN).  Chapter Three,
in addition to looking at regional regulation, also examines such international regulatory
collaborations.
Europe is increasingly co-operating and competing with China and India, two major
emerging economies that are also keen to develop their S&T sectors.  It is arguable that
new interdependencies between global actors require innovative global approaches to
S&T policy, or at least, a recognition of different local approaches to a global science.
Of course, this begs the wider question: Can there ever be such a thing as a ‘global
approach’?
Chapter Six examines issues arising from the universalist approach, such as so-
called universal values being labelled paternalistic,20 or else described as a new form of
neo-colonialism21 thought to undermine human dignity as well as cultural pluralism.22

3.  Increased public participation?
This thesis looks at the use of participatory Technology Assessment (pTA) in S&T
evaluation, a trend that has grown since the 1980s in the EU.  pTA can be defined as a
drive towards incorporating social concerns into technology assessment through public
dialogue incorporating a greater use of laypersons.  This trend has been driven by
increased public scepticism of scientific research and development.24  Reports of public

dissatisfaction in China following various food safety scandals over milk and gutter oil
confirm that scepticism about (a lack of) regulation is not confined to the EU.
The outcome has been a demand for more informed public debate, in addition to
greater public involvement in how new technologies should be regulated and funded), as
well as how they should be applied to everyday life.25  Policymakers in the EU anxious not

to repeat the mistakes associated with the introduction of biotechnology initiatives like
genetically modified (GM) foods – namely, that legislation came too late and with too little
public engagement and ethical reflection – began to call for the inclusion of ethical and

Chapter  Four looks at the pTA ‘nanofora’ that have been attempted thus far in the EU
and China (the latter being somewhat less concerned with  this approach  as yet), and

Discourse ethics has developed around Habermas’s argument that social order
depends on our capacity to recognize, through rational discourse, the intersubjective
validity of different views.  It aims to be a consensual ethics, in which only those norms
and actions can claim legitimacy that have been subjected to discourse, and when a non-
coercive consensus by all affected has been achieved.  Thus Habermas claims that
something can be valid when the foreseeable ‘consequences and side-effects of its
general observance for the interests and value-orientations of each individual could be
jointly accepted by all concerned without coercion’.28  Communicative or discourse action

attempts to coordinate purposive action rationally, so that all might come to a reasoned
agreement about the truth of a statement or of the rightness of a norm.29

The principles Habermas sees as requisite for dialogue are very similar to those of
pTA, particularly those of inclusivity and range of representation.  Commenting on

Nanotechnology is often examined not only in terms of its potential and practical
applications, but also for its transformative potential.  Under the heading of nanotechnology
we tend to think of engineering at the scale of the very small; however, we may also
remember utopian (or dystopian) visions, such as that in Eric Drexler’s 1986 Engines of
Creation, of tiny assemblers capable of creating any desired macroscopic object.  With
such technology we could, theoretically, create anything, a concept explored by Neal
Stephenson in his novel The Diamond Age (1995), which depicted a world of ubiquitous
nanotech where molecular assemblers can create basic goods, free to anyone who
requests them, thus eradicating starvation and homelessness.8

It is a vision of ‘nanotech synthesizers in factories, then restaurants, and finally in
homes,’ of foods that ‘could simply be synthesized cooked, with no need for a stove’, while
the dishes are also ‘synthesized along with the food, and then simply dropped dirty into the
recycler.’9  This kind of future could enable consumers to enjoy not only plentiful, but

tastes: ‘thousands of nanocapsules containing flavour or colour enhancers, or added
nutritional elements (such as vitamins), would remain dormant in the food and only be
released when triggered by the consumer.’10

allow the building of a ‘space elevator’ to move people and materials out of earth's orbit.  In

Approaching nanoethics
The role of nanoethics is ‘to engage in conversation with others about what kind of
world should be constituted’.47

When approaching the issue of the effects of a new technology, one standard approach is
that of ‘ELSI’, which examines the ‘ethical, legal and societal implications’ of new
technology.  This acronym appeared in 1989 in the West as part of the Human Genome
Project, the basic goal of such an approach being to forestall adverse effects associated
with biotechnology, to sponsor research and conferences, and also to make policy
recommendations.  The temptation for commentators on nanotechnology’s implications for
society has been to add an ‘N’ at the start – hence a ‘NELSI’ approach.48

This makes it sound a little easier than it is, as one issue with nanotechnology is not
merely its extensive reach of applications, or the idea of ‘adverse effects’, but its
‘unknowable’ quality – something that commentators have even labelled ‘noumenal’ (more
intellectually than empirically understood).  Nanotechnology may also require a paradigm
shift in the way we think about it; such a new science may require a radically new
approach, for ‘noumenal technology recedes into the uncanny otherness of nature and
resists our attempts to make it an object of experience and knowledge.’49  Thus Dupuy and

Grinbaum argue for insufficiency in all of the three main, traditional theoretical approaches
(of consequentialism, virtue ethics, and deontology):
Virtue ethics is manifestly insufficient since the problems ahead have very little to do
with the fact that scientists or engineers are beyond moral reproach or not.
Deontological doctrines do not fare much better since they evaluate the rightness of
an action in terms of its conformity to a norm or a rule... As for consequentialism –
i.e. the set of doctrines that evaluate an action based on its consequences for all
agents concerned - it treats uncertainty as does the theory of expected utility, namely
by ascribing probabilities to uncertain outcomes.50

Can one have an ethical debate about technologies that do not yet fully exist?51 Does

1.1. Hypothetical nanoethics?  Science fiction and nanotechnology

Mind uploading would be a fine thing, but I’m not convinced what you’d get at the end
of it would be even remotely human.64

We begin our discussion of nanoethics, and our eventual discussion of how Eastern and
Western approaches to the issue reflect differing ethics with a quick trip through nano-
themes as handled by science fiction writers in the West.  It should be noted that (as
discussed in the Introduction) for the purposes of this thesis, by ‘West’ I refer chiefly to the
EU but also at times briefly to the US, and by ‘East’ principally to China.
Richard Feynman has suggested that the scientific and visionary aspects of
nanotechnology have been interconnected from the beginning.65  Science fiction can in

some of its incarnations, such as satiric texts, for example, be an effective forum for ethical

casting them in fresh light.66

Of course, the opposite view can be argued.  Detractors suggest that this
speculative focus can distract from current realities,71  that ‘most nanoethics is too

futuristic… at the expense of ongoing incremental developments that are more ethically
significant’.72  Gordijn argues that utopian or apocalyptic visions impede nanoethics in their

such speculative debates is a short-circuiting of logic, whereby the unlikely becomes
inevitable.74

Despite this criticism, science fiction's exploration of more speculative aspects of
nanotechnology might at the very least afford a useful insight into the public's perception of
this complex technology.  In an analysis of UK media coverage of nanotechnology over a
15-month period (2003-4), the most prevalent reference was to Michael Crichton’s novel
Prey, which features deadly nanoswarms.75  Although Crichton’s critical gaze appears

chiefly aimed at profiteering corporations, the image of a woman controlled by a devouring
technology that exhibits predatory swarm behaviour is a sobering image of the destructive
consequences of rushing headlong into a new technology.

Nanofiction can usefully depict those pressing ethical issues that require consideration,
delineating areas of concern and offering hypothetical scenarios that highlight
contemporary problems.  This can help in encouraging or directing public debate. Such
issues become quickly apparent from any brief analysis of the last two decades of science
fiction, nanotechnology having become a theme in the 1990s in Western literature after its
early minimal appearance in such texts as Arthur C.Clarke’s1956 story ‘The Next Tenants’,
describing tiny machines that operate on a microscale, or Robert Silverberg’s 1969 short
story ‘How It Was when the Past Went Away’, which shows a form of nanotechnology
being used in the construction of loudspeakers.

One should first note however that such an analysis is of limited use for the
purposes of this thesis and its comparison of Chinese/EU attitudes to nanotechnology.
This is due to the fact that Eastern science fiction is a rather different genre.  If one
compares Western science fiction novels from the US and the UK with those published in
China, it immediately becomes apparent that the latter are not necessarily a useful
speculative forum.  As in Russia, China has struggled with a genre that simultaneously
promotes technological superiority and innovation, while also showing a deep level of
satire.  There is a certain nervousness in China even when it comes to time travel TV
shows, criticised for promoting ‘feudalism, superstition, fatalism and reincarnation’.76  Two

recent science fiction novels from China, Han Song’s 2066: Red Star over America (2000),
and Chan Koonchung’s The Fat Years (2009), thus only cautiously examine China’s
superpower status.  Liu Cixin perhaps conceals his message within a depiction of aliens’
attempts to control the minds of the Chinese populace in his trilogy Three Bodies (2007-
2011).
The East does have a tradition of translating classic science fiction novels from
English – Jules Verne being one popular choice.  Yet Verne’s popularity in the East is
probably due to the way his novelistic style adapts well to the ‘industrial’ focus of Chinese
science fiction, i.e. that celebrates technology rather than tackling ethical problems.77

(a)  Lotus-eating in the nanofuture
It is conceivable that the best-known novel on nanotechnology, apart from Crichton’s Prey,
is Neil Stephenson’s The Diamond Age (1995), already mentioned as depicting a world of
ubiquitous nanotech where molecular assemblers can create basic goods that are freely
distributed to anyone that requests them.  Yet Stephenson’s world of abundant nanotech is
socially stratified and stagnant.  In such a world of plenty, there is little to strive for – apart
from the freedom denied to the poor, kept docile through nanomanufactured goods and
denied any say in their lives.  Similar to Stephenson’s vision of autocratic Victorians,
Charles Stross’ Singularity Sky (2003) depicts the ‘New Republic's iron grip on its populace
as enabled through having control of so-called 'cornucopia machines’, which are a type of
nanotech assembler factory.  For both of these novels, nanotechnology in the form of
molecular assembly seems to be the modern equivalent of the Roman Empire’s bread and
circuses, intended to keep a population well-fed and docile.
Interestingly for the purposes of this thesis (although digressive in this current
discussion), Stephenson introduces occasional references to the clash of Western and
Eastern cultures.  A character remarks at one point how ‘poisonous’ Western technology

poison of opium, we could not open our lives to Western technology without taking in
Western ideas, which have been as a plague (sic) on our society. The result has

The nano-doomsday scenario will be familiar to readers of pulp fiction, or watchers of B-
movies in which cackling scientists maniacally work on destructive devices.  Although there
are some positive texts, such as Damien Darby’s Nano Saviour (2012), in which
nanomachines create an artificial intelligence that restores ecological stability, science
fiction writers opt for more destructive and dystopian nanofutures – probably because
impending disaster makes for a more thrilling plot.  Drexler’s famous end-of-the-world
scenario is fairly popular; arguing that molecular assembly should be treated with caution,
as assembler-based life forms, being more efficient than natural organisms, could destroy
the biosphere.  He even suggests that runaway nanotechnology could turn the universe
into ‘grey goo’ (although in fact he uses the image of dust to signify the state of matter once
the biosphere has been consumed, a state that is indeed probably grey, but not particularly
gooey).  Other writers have replicated this scenario in various doom-laden ways. Kurt
Vonnegut’s 1962 Cat’s Cradle hypothesises a form of nano-permutation of water called
'ice-nine', that is solid at room temperature, and which inevitably gets released into the
environment, bringing about the end of the world.80  And in Walter Jon Williams’ Aristoi

(1992), nano-apocalypse has already occurred – the universe is on its ‘backup version’,
post the incident of ‘Mataglap Nano’,  a gray goo-style disaster which originated in
Indonesia.

The most prevalent form of human enhancement in Western science fiction relates
to what is called ‘NBIC’ convergence. NBIC, as the acronym has it, refers to the
convergence of the disciplines of nanotechnology, biology, IT and cognitive science.
At one end of the spectrum, it involves uploading consciousness into a computer,
while at the other it leads to nanotechnological engineering at neural levels, enhancing
cognition or consciousness through neural implants or some kind of brain computer.
Swiestra et al have utilised the convergence issue to interrogate whether existing
interpretative or cognitive frameworks would become deficient compared with enhanced
nano-consciousness.113  Dupuy goes further to say that as cognitive science takes the

leading role in NBIC, it effectively becomes a research program examining new methods of
perceiving reality.114

Yet what might be lost if humanity were to evolve into cyborgism, becoming heavily
reliant on technology?  One answer comes from Kathleen Goonan’s Queen City Jazz
(1994), the first nanotech novel.  Noonan’s ‘nanotech cycle’ of Queen City Jazz, Mississippi
Blues (1997), the prequel Crescent City Rhapsody (2000), and Light Music (2002),
examines the issue of threats to identity from nanotechnology.  In Queen City Jazz,
Goonan’s futuristic Cincinnati is a place where huge bio-engineered bees carry information
through the streets, and enormous nanotech energy-producing flowers burst from the tops
of strange buildings. It also depicts an ‘NBIC’ future, in which uploaded consciousnesses
form part of a hive or group mind.  The  ‘information nanos’ designed to educate, and
described as ‘cheap and easy brain growth for the masses’, lead to a future lacking in
humanity, freedom, and individuality.115  The problem is not entirely technological in

Goonan’s novel; instead it is the result of a hubristic scientist's reach exceeding his grasp.
The nanoarchitect’s desire to keep his mother alive leads him to upload her into the city
mind, creating a tyrannical queen bee who rules the city.  The moral of the story is of
course that humanity is probably not to be trusted with the tool of nanotech.  Our emotions,
which arguably make us human, may lead us into error.  Thus Goonan suggests that

1.2 Nanoethics debates in the EU and in China
Either the ethics of NT (nanotechnology) will catch up or the science will slow
down.128

Bioethics does not serve society well simply by promoting a respect for other
cultures. That’s nice, but not enough. It better promotes society by helping to develop
the criteria and standards for knowing which practices and values should be
accepted and affirmed, which simply tolerated, and which rejected.129

The mainstreaming of debates about nanotechnology in the West is due in part to the
publication of reports by Greenpeace, the Royal Society and Royal Academy (RS/RAE),
and insurance company Swiss Re in 2003-4.  The first of these called for greater public
debate so as to ensure the environmental benefits and risks of nanotechnology were
understood, the second looked at chemical regulation and general socio-ethical issues, and
the third looked at nanoparticle risks.
One platform for nanoethics debates in the West is the journal NanoEthics: Ethics for
Technologies that Converge at the Nanoscale (Springer), begun in 2007.  Of course,
literature on nanoethics appeared well before that date, and Kjolberg and Wickson have
written a useful account of pre-2007 literature on the nanoethics field (1994-2006),
demonstrating a peak in publications during 2003.  Their database reveals four key areas
of interest in the EU and US. First, governance, the ‘processes and institutions for decision
making, regulation, legislation and public engagement.’130  Early discussion of the ethics of

nanotechnology in the EU and US has understandably tended to focus on risks to human
health and to the environment, a context that places an emphasis on determining whether
precautionary and regulatory measures are appropriate and efficient.  The other three
areas of particular interest defined by Kjølberg and Wickson were:
Perception: examining how nano is understood, presented, talked about and imaged.
Science: exploring the practice of nano S&T [Science & Technology] development
and instrumentation. Philosophy: engaging questions of metaphysics, the
natural/artificial and ethical norms.131

Abstract:
Towards a Global Ethics:  The Debate on Nanotechnology in
the European Union and China

The primary aim of the thesis is to assess whether ethical governance of Science
and Technology is feasible as a global approach, using the example of
nanotechnology.
The thesis firstly compares ethical issues identified by stakeholders in China
and the EU relating to the rapid introduction of a potentially transformative
technology, namely nanotechnology.  Part One of this thesis explores how the
‘narratives’ of nanotechnology differ in each region, particularly given their different
bioethics contexts, and examines how specific concerns translate into policymaking.
In questioning whether Eastern and Western approaches to nanotechnology
governance can be aligned, one can observe that Europe is increasingly co-
operating and competing with China.  Such new interdependences between global
actors require new global approaches to S&T policy, including ethical governance.
Part Two of this thesis explores the concept of ‘global ethics’ and discusses
the feasibility of a global approach.  Given criticism of both universalism and
relativism, it is often argued that a universal approach that takes sufficient account of
local context cannot be developed.
On the assumption that global ethics are achieved by global actors, this
thesis looks at global agency.
The thesis connects discourse ethics and participatory Technology
Assessment (pTA), arguing that a version of Habermasian discourse ethics can
provide a theoretical framework for dialogue between West and East. Discourse
ethics has developed around Habermas’s argument that social order depends on our
capacity to recognize, through rational discourse, the intersubjective validity of
different views.  Habermas asks the basic question of global ethics, of how different
views (particularly of social order) can be universally recognized and agreed,
perhaps within an 'ideal community' of communication, one that may be global.
The thesis adds to Habermas’s discourse model, utilising virtue ethics as well
as the work of, for example, Taylor, Beck, Korsgaard and others on identity

ii

[PDF page 4]
formation.  It is argued that the significant factor in global ethics is the formation of
the agent’s moral identity, the formation of which requires one to go beyond one’s
context, to achieve an intercultural personhood.  Habermas (as do Taylor, Beck and
others) suggests identity as a dual concept, reflecting an interdependence of society
and one’s inner self.  This would mean that one can understand the cultural biases
inherent in any act of communication, while acting autonomously of such bias.
If such a model of dual identity/agency can be applied to the intercultural
dialogue on the governance of nanotechnology between East and West, it could
potentially provide a new tool or model within pTA.

Introduction: Towards a Global Ethics?  Science &
Technology Policy for Nanotechnology

Now nanotechnology had made nearly anything possible, and so the cultural role in
deciding what should be done with it had become far more important than imagining
what could be done with it.1

Our stubborn egocentricities lead us to believe that the world must be run according
to our own templates; that all would be well with the world if only it were populated
with people like us.  But our dehumanised apprehension of the familiar points directly
to the resolution.  Only when we come to understand, or even just acknowledge,
each other’s complexities can comprehension begin.  Only when we apprehend each
other as human...will the world begin to make sense.2

Nanotechnology has been described as equivalent to the development that kick-started
the industrial revolution;3 as a potential road to salvation for developing counties dealing

with issues of energy production, agricultural productivity enhancement, and water
treatment;4 but also as a Faustian bargain that may yet lead to global destruction.5

Although at present nanotechnology is used in a variety of products, ranging from skin
creams and food packaging to longer-lasting tennis balls and warmer socks, its potential is
as yet undefined (solar power for all!  A cure for cancer! Nanobots!), leading to both
utopian hype and dystopian dread.  Is it a form of miraculous engineering, a universal
nostrum, or a terrifyingly vague science that may ultimately reduce the universe to ‘grey

goo’?6  Or is it simply a new line of research that has already proved disappointingly
unable to live up to its potential?7

The facts are that nanotechnology will affect our lives (as indeed it already does
through products available on the market), and that surveys show it to be poorly
understood by the public in terms of its risks and benefits.8

An emerging science, nanotechnology provides an opportunity for the public to
work alongside researchers, corporations, and governments to attempt ethical
implementation.  It provides a test case for how the world might act given a technology that
could conceivably transform the global economy and provide solutions to major global
issues such as pollution, while potentially creating new environmental and health risks.
Nanotechnology, in particular, has been presented as a key site for experimenting with
novel forms of so-called upstream engagement, or efforts to engage members of the
public in dialogue about emerging technologies.9  It provides a context for the emergence

of a new risk governance paradigm, in terms of which local societies' political cultures and
risk perceptions become significant factors in risk assessment and governance, with
conventional top-down/authoritative decision-making models now taking more notice of
public risk discourse.10

How might the world act together to inculcate ethical concerns into nanopolicy as it is
formulated across the globe?  This broad question may seem both idealistic and futile, yet
it is only a restatement of a much older question about how to ensure that new
technologies affect us only with our consent.

This question raises several others:
(1) What are the particular and/or new ethical concerns that might be raised by a
new technology such as nano?
(2) How do we work together globally to agree on such concerns?
(3) And who is ‘we’? What skills and processes are required for such global
participation?

Given these 3 questions, encompassing a discussion of nanoethical issues, another of
global cooperation, and also of ‘skills and processes’, it is useful to be clearer regarding
the intent of this thesis. The study contributes, firstly, to a comparative understanding of
the environments within which nanotechnology is ‘regulated’ and discussed within China
and the EU.  Part I of this thesis (Chapter 1-3) thus offers a case study of (dis)similarity.
Part II of the thesis (Chapters 4-6) looks at how global ethics (given these differences)
might work, offering a proceduralist model, one of pTA (participatory Technology
Assessment).
The primary aim of this thesis is to provide an expanded pTA model, given my
premise that global ethics is best done through global agents in pTA. Habermasian
thought allows the expansion of current pTA models to predicate how agents might
achieve consensus – perhaps even global consensus (as Habermas’s ‘universalisation
principle’ suggests).
Nanotechnology as a globally significant new technology provides a useful case
study against which to examine how pTA (nanofora, for example) might work within and
across differing cultures such as those of the EU and China. Given nanotechnology's
significance in both regions as central to economic growth, agreement on the ethical
impact on society of such a potentially radical new technology would seem to be of
considerable importance.

1.  New concerns?
The first question is a very broad one, encompassing issues of military usage, distributive
justice (given that nanotechnology could have vast application in developing countries),
and risk management of toxicity, as well as more futuristic scenarios to do with human
enhancement.  No wonder that the range of potential nanotechnology applications has led
to debates about public involvement in decision-making.
