III. Real-World Scene Understanding with High Resolution Wide Field Simulated Retinal Prosthetic Vision 

3.1 Introduction 

The PRIMA subretinal prosthesis is a vision restoration device that is currently being used in a clinical trial with patients (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2022). Until researchers can develop a device with less artificial, easier to interpret vision, the sparse patient population, invasiveness of the surgical procedure, potential safety risks, and artificiality of currently available devices limit the promise of visual prostheses to restore vision (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Levy et al., 2023; Nadolskis et al., 2024; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). One advantage of using simulations to understand perception with prosthetic vision is the ability to test multiple design iterations of currently available and future prosthetic devices simultaneously (Kasowski et al., 2023). Simulations can be used in studies by modeling cortical prostheses for cases when only the higher visual pathway is accessible (area V1 or higher, no functioning retina or optic nerve) (Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). Retinal prostheses, such as PRIMA, Argus II, and the Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal devices have been tested in hundreds of patients (compared to the relatively smaller population of cortical implant recipients) (Finn et al., 2020; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Karapanos et al., 2021; Muqit et al., 2023). Researchers have reported that patients with retinal devices can perceive light and have measurable improvements in visual acuity (letter, grating, or Landolt C) (Ayton et al., 2014; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020), however these improvements are limited and vary from patient to patient, 

> 55

leading to device abandonment (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Pérez Fornos et al., 2012). Many patients still have no measurable acuity when the device is turned on, such as those with Argus II (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Rachitskaya et al., 2020). Retinal prostheses are also designed to target a specific patient group based on cause of blindness. PRIMA is designed for patients with CVL and the device’s electrodes act by replacing the damaged photoreceptors that target the underlying bipolar cells (Palanker et al., 2022). The bipolar cells remain intact for cases of age-related macular degeneration, which is a disease condition that leads to CVL. The location of the electrode array on the retina is also specific to the cause of blindness. For example, since age-related macular degeneration patients have vision loss in the center of their retina due to central scotomas, PRIMA is implanted in the foveal region at the subretinal layer (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2022). The epiretinal Argus II and Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal Retinal devices were designed for patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP aka PVL or ‘tunnel vision’), so these arrays were implanted in the visual periphery and targeted the retinal ganglion cell layer (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Karapanos et al., 2021). By specifying a retinal implant design type and location, we can better relate the perceptual effects to the cause and retinal area of blindness. One study that tested patients implanted with PRIMA reported an increase in letter acuity for 29 out of 38 participants (Muqit 2025 ARVO abstract). Earlier studies show improvements in acuity with a smaller sample of PRIMA participants (n = 3) and report that patients were able to read letters, words, and signs with the device 

> 56

turned on (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020, 2022). The best reported acuities with the PRIMA device turned on ranged from 20/460 - 20/550 (1.37 - 1.44 logMAR) or 43.3 ETDRS letters (correct-to-normal acuity would be 20/20 Snellen, 0 logMAR, or 70 ETDRS) (Elliot et al., 1995). While promising, the extent to which visual prosthesis can fully restore functional vision is not well understood. PRIMA is roughly 7 degrees visual angle in diameter (2 mm in width) which is larger than the human foveola (1 degree visual angle diameter) but smaller than the typical scotoma size associated with later stages of age-related macular degeneration (diameter of 8.6 degrees visual angle) resulting in a smaller than natural field of view that can be conveyed by the device (Fletcher et al., 2012; Palanker et al., 2022; Tuten & Harmening, 2021; Whittaker et al., 1988). Results with patients using PRIMA suggest that when the device is turned on, patients see a small, prosthetic-filled aperture surrounded by the scotoma, but their natural peripheral vision beyond the scotoma’s eccentricity is intact (Palanker et al., 2020, 2022). While a larger prosthetic device could contribute to better perception overall, previous work has been unable to answer this question due to small form factors for devices likely necessary to maximize surgery success and minimize safety risks for patients. The visual prosthetic device with the largest field of view due to stimulation coverage is the Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal Retinal device at 38 by 28° visual angle (Karapanos et al., 2021). The device design is based on an earlier prototype that was smaller in size (19.44 by 19.2° visual angle) and limited to 24 electrodes (Petoe et al., 2017). 

> 57

Each device has a set number of electrodes (sometimes referred to as channels or pixels) with a given width. The size and number of electrodes could also influence perceptual clarity from visual prostheses. PRIMA arrays contain 378 hexagonal electrodes that are 100 μm in width (for comparison, a fovea with 1 degree visual angle diameter is approximately 288 μm). Another reason why perception with visual prostheses is degraded is due to technological limitations in engineering electrodes at a small enough size to mimic individual photoreceptors. Human cone photoreceptors have widths of 1 - 1.2 μm and send signals to receptive fields of bipolar cells (Mustafi et al., 2009). Larger fields of view and higher resolution displays benefit many aspects of visual perception, including making targets and hazards easier to detect (De Souza & Tartz, 2024; Shahar et al., 2010). Eye and head movements are ubiquitous in nature to facilitate perception and action, and become more restricted with increased PVL (Gegenfurtner, 2016; Titchener et al., 2019). When field of view is restricted, observer eye movements are restricted or altered, such as under CVL and PVL conditions (Guadron, Titchener, Abbott, Ayton, van Opstal, et al., 2023; Loschky et al., 2019; Nuthmann & Canas-Bajo, 2022; Yu & Kwon, 2023). For example, sighted participants under simulated PVL have better scene categorization performance when their field of view is larger than 10° visual angle (i.e. peripheral scotoma border eccentricity has not extended past 10° visual angle) (Loschky et al., 2019). This is supported by other examples in which smaller fields of view (less than 4 - 6° visual angle) resulted in worse performance for a visual search and reading tasks (Nuthmann & Canas-Bajo, 2022; Yu & Kwon, 2023). 

> 58

How future prostheses users would benefit from a larger device with increased field of view or a device of comparable size with a higher number of electrodes is not well understood. Manufacturing visual prostheses requires a substantial amount of resources, prototyping, and strict safety regulation after production (Borda & Ghezzi, 2022; Fernandez, 2018). One study tested PRIMA models of low and high resolutions (100 μm and 75 μm widths respectively, 100 μm is the size implanted in humans) in rats and found that a higher number of electrodes with higher resolution would increase acuity, suggesting that an updated PRIMA with those features would be beneficial for patients (B.-Y. Wang et al., 2022). Research with human participants to test effects of prosthetic fields of view and resolution is limited to simulations. Other SPV studies reported that a larger field of view increased reading speed, object recognition, and depth perception performance (E. Ho et al., 2019; Thorn et al., 2020). Previous studies that manipulated phosphene resolution and density for SPV also showed that higher resolutions led to better performance and faster response times in acuity and letter discrimination, face recognition, and sentence reading tasks (E. Ho et al., 2019; Killian et al., 2016). The findings from Ho et al. (2019), in which field of view (7° and 12°) and resolution (30, 60, and 100 μm) were manipulated in the same experiment, provided evidence that wider fields of view and higher resolutions led to better performance (E. Ho et al., 2019). Researchers have characterized the various spatial and temporal features of prosthetic vision to be used as computational models for tasks such as face recognition and scene segmentation (An et al., 2025; Avraham et al., 2021; Fine & Boynton, 2024; Park et 

> 59

al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024), but behavioral data is needed to validate how prosthetic viewing conditions impact perception. Psychophysical data from patients with the Argus I and Argus II and the first and second generation suprachoroidal retinal devices provided some insight as to how improvements in device designs with increased surface area and smaller electrodes should increase the quality of the image (Caspi, 2009; Dorn et al., 2013; Petoe et al., 2017, 2025; Shivdasani et al., 2017; Yue et al., 2020). Importantly, one study tested a patient implanted with Argus I in the right eye and Argus II in the left eye reported that there was no measurable advantage in visual function between the two, but the Argus II allowed for improved spatial visual ability over the Argus I according to patient reports (Yue et al., 2020). While direct comparisons between generations of devices remains limited, simulations of retinal prostheses serve a fast, low cost option to begin addressing these questions. State of the art visual prostheses do not integrate eye movements (Fernandez, 2018). Patients are forced to rotate their head to update the scene camera on the glasses, causing a perceptual incongruency resulting in the overall image appearing distorted in space and time independent of electrical stimulation alone (Fernandez, 2018; Paraskevoudi & Pezaris, 2019, 2021). Caspi et al. (2018, 2021) modified the Argus II and Orion to record and integrate eye movements by using the recorded eye movement data as feedback for the camera, showing how eye movements affect the perceived location of phosphenes and can shift the camera’s region of interest. They found that patients with Argus II were more accurate at localizing a white circular target when a dynamic region of interest was 

> 60

used to enhance the camera image (Caspi et al., 2018). Evaluating how prosthetic viewing conditions influence eye movements in combination with perception is necessary to convey naturalistic perception with electrical stimulation. Similar to how patients who are blind and/or have low vision are referred to vision rehabilitation with assistive technology, blind patients who are implanted with a visual prosthesis will require time, experience, and training to get maximum benefit of their device (Bowman & Liu, 2017; Chen et al., 2009; Geruschat et al., 2016). The visual perception that visual prostheses provide requires successful interpretation of phosphenes: percepts of light that are not elicited by natural light stimulation but instead by electricity or pressure (any method of electrical stimulation mentioned in this work refers to the method used in devices like PRIMA and Argus II for this manuscript) (Beauchamp et al., 2020; Fernandez, 2018; Liu et al., 2022). Results from previous studies testing patients implanted with Argus II and the second generation (44-channel) suprachoroidal implants have found that users performed better at visual function tasks (Da Cruz et al., 2016; Dorn et al., 2013; Muqit et al., 2023; Petoe et al., 2025; Rachitskaya et al., 2020) and activities of daily living (Dagnelie et al., 2017; Geruschat et al., 2016; Karapanos et al., 2021) with their devices turned on. Patients learned how to use their visual prostheses over 68 weeks of testing for visual orientation, social interactions, and more, with notable limitations for moving objects (Dagnelie et al., 2017; Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Karapanos et al., 2021). One study that tested sighted participants under simulated thalamic vision for reading found significant improvements in speed and accuracy after 8 weeks of 

> 61

training (Rassia & Pezaris, 2018). A different study by Killian and Pezaris (2016) tested non-human primates with SPV and showed that letter discrimination performance improved after hundreds of thousands of trials of training with a range of phosphene densities and letter acuities (Killian et al., 2016). Previous work studying patients with low vision have found that training can also lead to improvements in performance. For example, Janssen and Verghese (2016) have found that training patients with CVL on a visual search task for six hours led to faster saccades and reductions in response times for a same/different judgement task without impacting accuracy, highlighting the role of training eye movements in perception for low vision viewing conditions (Janssen & Verghese, 2016). A different study by Maniglia et al. (2020) found that training CVL patients with contrast detection and fixation stability tasks led to improvements in acuity, faster reading speeds, and reduced crowding effects, suggesting that training can generalize to other visual functions. Theories from perceptual learning and findings from training experiments suggest that task difficulty is sensory specific (Biles et al., 2023; Karapanos et al., 2021; Killian et al., 2016; Lu & Dosher, 2022; Maniglia et al., 2020; Rassia & Pezaris, 2018). Patients who are blind, have low vision, or have a visual prosthesis are supervised by occupational therapists and orientation and mobility specialists to learn how to integrate other senses for safe navigation (Bowman & Liu, 2017; Geruschat et al., 2016; Karapanos et al., 2021; Rachitskaya et al., 2020). While challenging due to vision loss, completing daily activities such as navigating a busy street intersection and identifying faces can be trained for patients with vision loss 

> 62

(Bowman & Liu, 2017; Calabrèse et al., 2018) and patients with prosthesis (Rachitskaya et al., 2020). Until prosthetic devices allow for better perception, the specific roles they play as an assistive technology to improve functional vision need to be better understood to complement individual patient needs (Kasowski et al., 2023; Nijboer, 2015). To evaluate how a subretinal prosthesis would influence perception and address limitations for future devices, we had sighted participants view and describe real-world scenes with a simulated subretinal prosthesis while their eye movements were recorded. Similar to the work in Johnson et al. 2025, participants looked at scenes with one or three saccades under simulated prosthetic vision (SPV), CVL, or control conditions. The goal of the study was to determine how the field of view and resolution impact perception by evaluating semantic quality of descriptions and fixation patterns. We hypothesize that a wider field of view with higher resolution will lead to description ratings and information sampling behavior similar to controls, with narrow field of view and low resolution leading to worse ratings and more varied eye movements. Given that patients require training and experience to use their device at full potential, we conducted a follow up study to determine if it is possible to improve scene understanding with SPV. In our follow up study, we hypothesize that SPV with narrow field of view and low resolution will lead to larger improvements in learning to understand and describe scenes compared to wider field of view and high resolution. We predict that participants will improve with SPV by learning to either interpret the

Abstract The Effects of Low and Prosthetic Vision on Scene Understanding: Relating Semantic Information with Eye Movements and Plasticity by Byron A. Johnson Age - related macular degeneration (ARMD) and retinitis pigmentosa (RP) are two leading causes of adventitious chronic blindness with no known cure. Both conditions involve the development of bilateral overlapping scotomas in which parts of the retina are degraded while the remaining retina is spared (Ito et al., 2022; Ying et al., 2008). ARMD and RP viewing conditions (central and peripheral vision loss respectively) negatively impact perception and eye movements for acuity, reading, visual search, depth perception, face recognition, scene gist categorization, and more (Bittner & Ferraz, 2020; Janssen & Verghese, 2016; Seiple et al., 2013; Timmis et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2010; Verghese et al., 2021). Visual prostheses have been tested as potential solutions to restore vision for people with advanced forms of ARMD and RP (Da Cruz et al., 2016; Muqit et al., 2023). While testing patients can provide a ground truth for understanding how vision loss and restoration affects perception, recruiting patients (especially those with visual prostheses) for studies can be challenging. Evaluation of prosthetic device designs can only be performed after a patient has been implanted, which is invasive, resource intensive, and differs largely from natural vision (Chen et al., 2009; xii Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021) . Implant sizes are relatively small, resulting in a small field of view (Fletcher et al., 2012; Palanker et al., 2022; Thorn et al., 2020). The individual electrode widths of these devices are also much larger than the retinal cells they intend to replace, limiting the maximum resolution required for natural vision (Ho et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022). All current prosthesis designs use a camera that is fixed to frames worn by the user, forcing users to make head movements while suppressing eye movements and further worsening the resulting perception (Caspi et al., 2018; Paraskevoudi & Pezaris, 2021). Future visual prosthesis recipients would benefit from training and learning compensatory strategies that can improve perception. Image processing techniques have been developed as visual display simulators to test the effects of low and prosthetic vision on perception. When combined with gaze - contingent processing, simulators allow for measuring compensatory eye movement behaviors associated with perception. Prosthetic vision simulators also allow researchers to iterate features based on relative best performance. While previous simulation work has measured the effect of low vision and prostheses on perception, few studies have compared more than one viewing condition (Loschky et al., 2019; Nuthmann & Canas-Bajo, 2022; Pollmann et al., 2020; Yu & Kwon, 2023). In order to address these gaps in the literature, two experiments will be designed and tested using gaze - contingent visual display simulations. Chapter 1 is a brief literature review on how low and prosthetic vision affect perception and eye movements, including examples of studies in which training led to improvements. 

> xiii

Chapter 2 tests the effects of simulated vision loss on rapid scene understanding for 120 real-world photos, specifically comparing the effects of ARMD and RP (central vision loss and peripheral vision loss respectively) on the same task. We find that simulations of central and peripheral vision loss worsen scene understanding in different ways. Peripheral vision loss leads to worse descriptions while central vision loss results in varied eye movements compared to control participants. We also find that the type of scene matters: scenes that contain people behaving and interacting with other people and objects led to bigger differences in effects compared to scenes that lacked interactions. Chapter 3 details a second (two part) experiment that involves simulating prosthetic vision to evaluate how visual prosthesis affects scene understanding. The first phase of experiment 2 tested the initial effects of prosthetic vision on scene understanding and eye movements. We assigned participants to one of six different viewing conditions: controls (no simulation), central vision loss, and four prosthesis designs with either combination of wide or narrow field of view and high or low resolution. The second phase will evaluate if participants in the three worst prosthesis conditions can learn and adapt to their simulated prosthetic condition by improving scene understanding ability over time with 12 hours of training. While a wide field of view and high resolution device was expected to yield the best prosthetic perception, descriptions generated with the wide field of view and high resolution condition were only slightly better than narrower field of view and lower resolution conditions. For learning effects, we find that training participants with 600 novel real-world scenes can lead to improved (but not perfect) scene understanding 

> xiv

and that participants can learn to adapt their eye movements while using simulated prosthesis without explicit instruction. The ways in which perception and eye movements deviated from viewing training scenes with no simulation to viewing test scenes with simulation depended on the assigned condition. Results from phase 2 show that the narrow field of view high resolution condition led to descriptions with higher ratings compared to wide or narrow field of view with low resolution. Participants in the wide field of view with low resolution condition initially show larger saccade amplitudes with longer latencies compared to narrow field of view conditions of either resolution. With training, amplitudes were smaller and latencies were faster, suggesting that participants in the wide field of view low resolution condition are adapting their fixation strategy, but still miss important details in the scene. This work will allow for measurable predictions on the impact of low and prosthetic vision on scene understanding and compensatory eye movement behaviors. Results also provide insight as to how prosthetic device features, such as field of view and resolution, can have different perceptual effects and may require different training regimes for patients to reach their full abilities with the device.

I. Introduction 1.1 Perception and Eye Movements with Low Vision 

The number of people expected to be diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) in 2040 is 288 million (approximately 3 percent of the estimated world population) (Wong et al., 2014). The prevalence of retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is reported to be 1 in every 3000 - 5000 people (You et al., 2013; Zapf et al., 2015). There is currently no cure for either condition. ARMD and RP are two leading causes of blindness in which photoreceptor loss occurs within overlapping regions of both eyes. ARMD involves the loss of both rod and cone photoreceptors at or around the fovea, with rods being affected earlier and the affected region growing over time. People diagnosed with early forms of ARMD may have issues performing tasks in low light conditions (such as reading and driving). Advanced forms of ARMD result in worse visual acuity and eventually blindness (Jackson et al., 2002; Ying et al., 2008). RP is a different disease in which photoreceptors (mainly rods but subsequently cones) located in the periphery are affected. Acuity is spared in early stages of RP but the visual field is limited (i.e. ’tunnel vision’). The concentric area of affected photoreceptors increases over time and spreads inward towards the fovea and can also lead to blindness (Bittner & Ferraz, 2020; Ito et al., 2022; Menghini et al., 2020). Much work has gone into recruiting patients with these conditions to quantify how photoreceptor loss affects perception. Patients with binocular ARMD have been found to be less accurate and make inefficient saccades to already explored areas in visual search tasks compared to sighted controls (Verghese et al., 2021).The foveal 

> 1

scotoma (overlapping area of retina with degraded photoreceptors associated with ARMD) blocks vital information that would otherwise be perceived by the observer. Some patients have been shown to alter their saccade behaviors in order to fixate an object outside or on the border of the scotoma location, utilizing this peripheral location as a reference for fixation. Previous work has examined how eye movements and performance (such as visual search) can improve over time with a central scotoma (Janssen & Verghese, 2016). The peripheral vision loss associated with RP spares acuity in initial stages while limiting the visual field (Bittner & Ferraz, 2020). The peripheral scotoma in RP restricts eye movements required for executing behaviors such as path planning to avoid obstacles or navigate stairs (Angelopoulos et al., 2019; Timmis et al., 2017). Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity are also impacted by RP (Bittner & Ferraz, 2020). ARMD has been shown to affect perception and saccade behavior when compared to sighted participants. Verghese and colleagues (2016 and 2022) have studied the effect of ARMD on eye movements extensively (Janssen & Verghese, 2016; N. Shanidze et al., 2016; N. M. Shanidze et al., 2022; Verghese et al., 2021; Vullings et al., 2022). In one experiment, researchers were interested in measuring the relationship between patient scotoma locations and the ability to track the path of a moving target. In order to do this, individual patient scotomas were first mapped by presenting flashes of light at different locations on the retina to assess variations in retinal sensitivity (also known as microperimetry). Once the scotoma was mapped, participants completed a smooth pursuit task following a target circle and had their eye movements recorded. The researchers used a scanning laser ophthalmoscope 

> 2

(SLO) in order to visualize the target directly on the retina while monitoring eye movements. Results showed that eye movement behaviors varied depending on if the target moved towards or away from the scotoma. Pursuit gains (the rate of change in eye movement position over time) were lower when the target moved towards from the scotoma location. Median pursuit gains and latencies (i.e. reaction times) differed significantly between patients and controls, with patients showing less gains and longer latencies for following the target (N. Shanidze et al., 2016). Another study found that ARMD patients make larger saccades, have worse fixation stability, and are worse at following the target compared to controls (N. M. Shanidze et al., 2022). These findings explain how ARMD can impact daily tasks such as visual search, reading, and face recognition (Verghese et al., 2021). Changes in saccade behavior have also been measured in people with RP. Guadron and colleagues (2023) had participants with RP perform a horizontal saccade task in which the target could appear at varying distances either to the left or right of fixation (Guadron, Titchener, Abbott, Ayton, Van Opstal, et al., 2023). Control participants showed high correlations between target distance and saccade amplitude, however, RP participant correlations were significantly weaker than controls, suggesting that vision loss in the periphery led to very large goal-directed saccades. RP participants also showed longer latencies than controls. Guadron et al. (2023) also recruited ARMD participants within the same experiment and found similar effects of vision loss in the fovea: correlations between target eccentricity and saccade amplitude were lower and latencies were longer than controls. Guadron et al. (2023) reported that RP impacted performance on the horizontal saccade task 

> 3

more than ARMD. A different experiment conducted by Titchener et. al (2019) had participants with either early or late-stage RP view a real-world scene and perform a smooth pursuit task while their eye and head movements were recorded (Titchener et al., 2019). Eye and head movement recordings were combined for a third measure of overall gaze behavior. The probability of the fixation location of the eye at the end of a shift in gaze (customary oculomotor range, COMR) was calculated to characterize fixation stability for people with RP. Results showed that the late-stage RP group made fewer eye movements and made fewer shifts in gaze when viewing the real-world scene compared to the early stage RP and control participants. The degree of COMR was much smaller for RP patients, suggesting that head movements increase but eye movements decrease for people with RP (Titchener et al., 2019). 

1.2 Training and Vision Rehabilitation for Patients with Low Vision 

Previous research has studied how ARMD and RP patients can refine their saccades (and associated perceptual abilities) over time with training. For ARMD, much work has examined how patients tend to stop using their fovea (covered by the central scotoma) and instead use a peripheral locus for fixation: the patient uses their preferred retinal locus (PRL). Vullings et al. (2022) suggested that the inefficient ”backwards” saccades seen in visual search for people with ARMD may be linked to the new PRL located at the edge of the scotoma (Vullings et al., 2022). Notably, the authors claimed that all four of their ARMD participants had an ”established PRL” and that participants tended to place search targets on the border of the scotoma at the PRL location. In a different experiment, Maniglia, Soler, and Trotter (2020) 

> 4

recruited ARMD participants to see if training at PRL locations would improve perception. First, individual PRLs were localized using optical coherence tomography (OCT). Then, participants were trained using a contrast detection task in which they were instructed to use their PRL to fixate. In order to determine if training influenced performance over time, four transfer tests were taken at the beginning, middle, and end of training. Results showed that training led to lower contrast thresholds, better near visual acuities, reduced crowding effects, and faster reading speeds (Maniglia et al., 2020). Other training experiments for ARMD that encourage PRL use have found improvements in fixation stability, increases in search accuracy, and a reduction in search time (Hilal et al., 2021). Training patients with RP has been explored by Yoshida and Seiyama (2014 and 2022) (Yoshida et al., 2014; Yoshida & Seiyama, 2022). In one experiment, participants with RP were trained for eight to ten months using their remaining vision to fixate and track individual letters. A reading test and separate functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) test were conducted before and after training to see if training would improve performance or alter brain activity. While all RP participants performed worse at the reading test compared to controls, post-training reading scores improved for five out of six RP participants. Results from the fMRI test found increases in activity of the frontal eye fields for all patients, providing further evidence that training can influence cortical control of eye movements (Yoshida et al., 2014). A second experiment recruited twenty - seven participants with RP and recorded their eye movements while reading. Results showed that task performance differed based on the severity of RP: the late stage advanced RP group had more 

> 5

fixations, larger saccade amplitudes, longer reading times, and worse acuities compared to mild and healthy control groups (Yoshida & Seiyama, 2022). A third study by Ivanov et al. (2016) reported that training not only improved eye movements, but also increased walking speed for participants with RP (Ivanov et al., 2016). The results from training with ARMD and RP suggest that patients can learn efficient eye movement strategies to improve their perceptual performance, but also (1) the size and extent of the vision loss factors into performance and (2) training could improve the quality of life for patients (Hilal et al., 2021; Ivanov et al., 2016; Vullings et al., 2022; Yoshida & Seiyama, 2022). 

1.3 Perception and Eye Movements with Prosthetic Vision 

Sight restoration via electrical stimulation has been studied as a potential solution to ARMD and RP, both of which have no cure. The Argus II epiretinal device (Cortigent, formerly Second Sight Medical Products) is the most popular visual prosthesis with over 350 patients with RP from around the world successfully implanted (Finn et al., 2020). The PRIMA subretinal device (Pixium Vision) has been implanted in five people with ARMD (Muqit et al., 2023). Each visual prosthesis is designed to restore sight for a specific vision loss condition: currently only RP patients can qualify for Argus II and only ARMD patients can qualify for PRIMA. While both devices use similar methods to restore vision, the fact that they have to be surgically implanted at the retina disqualifies future users who become blind for reasons other than RP or ARMD (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Muqit et al., 2023). Cortical visual prostheses bypass the early visual system (i.e. retina and thalamus) and have the potential to provide sight restoration for many causes of blindness (Niketeghad & 

> 6

Pouratian, 2019). The ORION cortical device (Cortigent) is implanted onto the surface of the brain in order to stimulate the subdural layers of the visual cortex. ORION has been successfully implanted in six participants (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021). The Argus II, PRIMA, and ORION implants are three examples of a larger category of devices in development that claim to restore vision to people with blindness, however, the quality of vision provided by the current generation of visual prostheses is severely limited and unnatural (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Muqit et al., 2023; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019; Ramirez et al., 2023). Visual prostheses aim to restore vision by replicating the neural activity of natural vision via electrical stimulation (Levy et al., 2023; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019; Ramirez et al., 2023). The Argus II, PRIMA, and ORION devices all take in visual input with a camera mounted onto frames worn by the user. The camera feed is preprocessed to reduce clutter, then converted to electrical pulses with a computer, and finally transmitted to an array of electrodes that has been surgically implanted. The signal from the camera feed will activate electrodes determined by an object’s real world location and relative brightness (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Levy et al., 2023; Ramirez et al., 2023; B.-Y. Wang et al., 2022). The quality of this signal differs from natural vision in several ways. First, there is a limited amount of electrodes that can be fit to an implant. The resolution (maximum acuity) provided by current implant designs is much worse than the resolution of natural vision (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; E. Ho et al., 2019; Muqit et al., 2023; Stronks & Dagnelie, 2014; B.-Y. Wang et al., 2022). Second, electrical stimulation is typically too strong and can 

> 7

activate neighboring receptive fields (Beyeler et al., 2019; Finn et al., 2020). This effect causes the low resolution stimulus provided to appear as bright, white phosphenes (percepts caused by electrical or mechanical stimulation) in a black background (Beyeler et al., 2019; Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Levy et al., 2023; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). The phosphene images provided by electrode arrays produce a low - level distorted representation of the environment (Beyeler et al., 2019; Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Levy et al., 2023). Retinal implants and cortical implants differ based on the implantation site. The Argus II is implanted in the epiretinal layer, PRIMA in the subretinal layer, and ORION on the visual cortex (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Muqit et al., 2023; Ramirez et al., 2023). Epiretinal implants are designed to bypass the damaged photoreceptors and activate the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) leading to the optic nerve (Beyeler et al., 2019; Finn et al., 2020; A. C. Ho et al., 2015). The advantage of epiretinal implants is that they can potentially restore sight for cases in which all of the preceding layers of the retina are damaged. Subretinal implants are inserted closer to the photoreceptors in the inner nuclear layer. Subretinal implants use photodiodes instead of standard electrodes and are activated by light rather than an external computer. Subretinal implants can only work for cases of vision loss where the inner layers of the retina are still intact (Muqit et al., 2023; B.-Y. Wang et al., 2022) . Percepts with the Argus II epiretinal implant often appear as long streaks (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021). This is due to the elongated curved shape associated with RGC fibers (Beyeler et al., 2019). The PRIMA subretinal implant is smaller in size and requires a strong light source to activate the photodiodes. 

> 8

Cortical implants work similarly to retinal devices, but try to replicate cortical signals of visual processing (Levy et al., 2023; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). Cortical implants could be a potential solution for cases of blindness in which the visual cortex is still intact (Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019; Ramirez et al., 2023). Besides surgical risk, replicating brain activity of natural vision to activate visual responses is much less understood compared to retinal activity, making testing of cortical prostheses difficult (Liu et al., 2022). Cortical magnification also leads to distortion as electrodes placed at foveal areas of the cortex appear much larger than peripheral areas (Oswalt et al., 2021). One major advantage of cortical prostheses is that they could potentially be a cure for all types of blindness, however, surgical procedures for retinal prostheses are considered safer and can target earlier portions of the visual pathway making it easier to test retinal devices with patients. Previous work with patients that have an implant have provided some insight as to how well visual prostheses can restore vision. Erickson-Davis and Korzybska (2021) conducted semi-structured interviews with Argus II users about their perceptual experiences with the device. Users reported seeing ”bright crescent shapes”, described as ”small flash[es]”, sometimes ”flickering” or ”blinking”. One participant reported that Argus II ”doesn’t reflect light in the same way” as natural vision (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021). Other experiments offer quantitative results regarding perception with Argus II. While nearly half of the patients were able to have their acuity measured after years of using the device, the reported acuities were poor at best (2.5 logMAR or 20/6324 Snellen) (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Rachitskaya et al., 2020). This limit on acuity is likely due to the arrangement of 

> 9

electrodes. The Argus II has an array of 10 by 6 electrodes each with a diameter of 200 micrometers, totaling sixty pixels. The array itself takes up a large portion of the retina and often spans both the fovea and periphery, approximately 19 by 11 degrees visual angle (Luo & Da Cruz, 2016; Stronks & Dagnelie, 2014). The uniform arrangement of the electrode array means that the distinction between activating the fovea versus periphery is ignored and adds further distortion. The Argus II provides artificial vision that, while leading to better performance with the device ON compared to OFF, ultimately fails to provide functional vision that can help patients perform daily activities. Studies report Argus II patients having minimal success with localization, contrast detection, and motion detection (Castaldi et al., 2016; Dorn et al., 2013; A. C. Ho et al., 2015). Argus II users demonstrated limited success at other tasks using real life objects (and people) with the device on, such as: recognizing and reaching for objects on a table, sorting white and black socks, sidewalk navigation, and walking direction discrimination (Da Cruz et al., 2016; Kotecha et al., 2014). Many users expressed disappointment with the device and stopped using it after a couple of years (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021). The PRIMA subretinal implant has 378 electrodes (photodiode pairs) each with a diameter of 100 micrometers (half the size of Argus II electrodes). The PRIMA implant is 17 degrees visual angle and is smaller than Argus II (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020). Each device is implanted at each patient’s PRL (measured before implantation). PRIMA has several advantages: (1) smaller electrodes allow for improved resolution, (2) the location (center of retina) make it more useful as a retinal locus, (3) photovoltaic cells are activated by infrared light and update based 

> 10

on eye movements, (4) the subretinal location targets bipolar cells, avoids direct stimulation of RGCs, and even allows for use of remaining intact retina (users can see with a prosthetic ”fovea” and healthy ”periphery” that can be combined for perception) (Muqit et al., 2023; B.-Y. Wang et al., 2022). The PRIMA implant is much newer compared to the Argus II and will require more time before implanted participants can be recruited for experiments. Preliminary results after four years with three participants show that PRIMA improved mean visual acuities (logMAR 1.39 or Snellen 20/500) (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020). The ORION cortical prosthesis includes many of the same components as Argus II and is designed for cortical stimulation (Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019; Ramirez et al., 2023). The ORION implant has 60 electrodes that are 2000 micrometers in diameter (twenty times the size of PRIMA electrodes). Like retinal prostheses, vision perception with cortical prostheses is limited. Levy and colleagues (2023) interviewed four ORION users about their experience with the device. Participants reported that the artificial vision with ORION is unnatural and that learning to understand the vision takes much practice (Levy et al., 2023). Simultaneous stimulation of electrodes causes the phosphenes to combine, which can make it difficult to perceive the outlines of objects (Beauchamp et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022). Previous work has explored how sequential activation of electrodes can produce brighter phosphenes with more consistent locations compared to simultaneous activation (Oswalt et al., 2021; Salas et al., 2022). There is currently no record of measured visual acuity for ORION or any other cortical implant. 

> 11

A major limitation of all visual prostheses is the lack of integration of eye movements. Both retinal and cortical devices rely on stimulus input based on an external camera fixed to frames worn by the user (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Palanker et al., 2020; Paraskevoudi & Pezaris, 2019; Salas et al., 2022). Natural vision utilizes the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR, gaze stabilization for head movements) and the optokinetic reflex (OKR, combination of slow and fast eye movements for pursuit movement) to facilitate gaze and tracking respectively (Caspi et al., 2018; Paraskevoudi & Pezaris, 2019; Verghese et al., 2021). The camera input for all visual prostheses can only update via head movements, which creates a disconnect between eye and head movements typically seen with natural vision (Sabbah et al., 2014). Caspi and colleagues (2018) found that shifting the “region of interest” of the camera by integrating eye movement recordings improved target localization performance and reduced head movements for Argus II users (Caspi et al., 2018). Eight patients with Argus II were recruited to complete a pointing task while their eye movements were being recorded. Eye tracking was done with a second pair of glasses fitted in front of the Argus II frames. Calibration and localization tests were done with control of the camera stimulus (not video mode) based on distances between pupil and corneal reflections using infrared light (Caspi et al., 2018). The same setup was tested on two participants with cortical implants: one with ORION and a second sighted participant with epilepsy implanted with the NeuroPace Responsive Neurostimulator. Remapping of stimuli based on eye position improved localization for both participants (Caspi et al., 2021), further suggesting that future visual prostheses will need to utilize eye movements to direct the device camera. 

> 12

1.4 Training and Rehabilitation for Patients with Prosthetic Vision 

Training for visual prostheses has the potential to benefit users similar to training patients with low vision (Chen et al., 2009). The large implant device size, peripheral placement, poor resolution, and disconnect between head and eye movements show that current generation prostheses do not have the ability to restore natural vision (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Levy et al., 2023; Muqit et al., 2023) . While implanted patients have some light perception, they are required to learn how to reinterpret phosphene images. Vision loss and prosthetic vision are two forms of visual impairment with similar changes in degradation. Rehabilitation for vision loss has been studied and applied for centuries (Chen et al., 2009; Markowitz, 2016). Experiments with visual prostheses have been documented as early as the year 1918, however, few experiments have examined rehabilitation with a visual prosthesis (Liu et al., 2022). The longest record of training with a device is from the five year Argus II clinical trial with twenty users. Task performance was better with the device on, but improvements in acuity, localization, motion detection, and more were far from complete restoration (Da Cruz et al., 2016). Most prostheses users stop using their device because it fails to provide vision that can be used for daily activities (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Ramirez et al., 2023). Results from the five year study were for safety and visual function assessments, not for training or rehabilitation. Rachitskaya et al. (2020) addressed this by testing four Argus II patients with a Computer Assisted Rehabilitation Environment (CAREN) (Rachitskaya et al., 2020). Participants were recruited for eight rehabilitation 

> 13

sessions using the system which includes a large projection screen, multidirectional treadmill, motion capture camera, and hand rails for safety. A physical therapist was also present during tests. Participants completed standard visual function (acuity, localization, motion) and mobility (gait assessment and postural stability) tests. Results showed that all participants improved in localization and had faster walking speeds after the training (Rachitskaya et al., 2020). A secondary measure called the Functional Low-vision Observer Rated Assessment (FLORA) has been developed to measure how patients perform real life tasks with the device ON vs OFF. FLORA is measured with a trained vision rehabilitation specialist. Results with FLORA show how prostheses patients can make gradual improvements in orientation and mobility tasks over time (Da Cruz et al., 2016; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Karapanos et al., 2021). 

1.5 Scene Perception with Central and Peripheral Vision Loss 

A scene is a shared space that may (or may not) provide context to one or more object’s identity or relationship to other objects (Eckstein et al., 2017; Epstein & Baker, 2019). Scenes as stimuli can be used for free viewing without instruction or for vision based tasks such as visual search. Real-world scenes are irregular and more likely to include visual clutter, requiring observers to make multiple eye movements to acquire information. It has been suggested that humans process scenes based on a hierarchy of visual features determined by task relevance. Kadar and Ben-Shahar (2012) recruited seventy - nine sighted participants to categorize over 300 pairs of real-world scenes. The categories ranged from man made (bedroom, kitchen, street) to natural environments (coast, forest, mountain). Participant responses revealed a hierarchy in which decisions about man made 

> 14

versus natural categories were prioritized first, followed by decisions comparing indoor or outdoor scenes (Kadar & Ben-Shahar, 2012). Previous studies testing patients with low or prosthetic vision have used letters, gratings, objects, and people as stimuli for experiments (Da Cruz et al., 2016; Maniglia et al., 2020; Timmis et al., 2017) but studies have also included real-world scenes in order to understand how low or prosthetic vision affects perception of visual complexity (Janssen & Verghese, 2016; Peyrin et al., 2017; Thibaut et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2010; Vullings et al., 2022). Previous studies have shown that vision loss can negatively impact scene categorization. Tran et al. (2010) recruited twenty - seven patients with ARMD for a scene categorization task. Participants were instructed to categorize scenes as either natural or urban and indoor or outdoor. Participant scotomas were mapped using visual field testing and visual acuity was measured. Results showed that participants with ARMD were significantly less sensitive (lower d prime) and less accurate than controls at categorizing scenes. The size of the scotoma in ARMD participants had a significant correlation with response times when discriminating between indoor and outdoor scenes. Acuity was not associated with any other measure regarding scene perception (Tran et al., 2010). A different experiment by Peyrin et al. (2017) recruited ARMD participants for indoor versus outdoor scene categorization using filtered scenes. The images were processed by manipulating the spatial frequency of the scene while reducing either the luminance or contrast. ARMD participants made significantly more non-responses for categorization compared to controls, especially for scenes filtered for high spatial frequencies. 

> 15

ARMD participants made more errors for indoor scenes compared to outdoor scenes (Peyrin et al., 2017). Recording eye movements is another measure that can be used to understand how low and prosthetic vision affect scene perception. Thibaut et al. (2016) showed ARMD participants scenes, objects, and objects in scenes. ARMD participants had shorter fixation durations and made more saccades with larger amplitudes compared to controls for all three categories of stimuli (Thibaut et al., 2016). In the experiment by Titchener et al. (2019) participants with late RP made significantly less shifts in gaze and fewer eye movements compared to controls when passively viewing a video of a scene of traffic (Titchener et al., 2019). Given that real-world scenes are complex it is important to note how they have been used as different types of stimuli in studies testing patients. The experiments by Tran (2010) and Peyrin (2017) measured scene gist (the ability to rapidly categorize a scene based on its contents) (Peyrin et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2010). The experiments by Verghese and colleagues (2016 and 2022) used real-world scenes to understand how ARMD affects visual search. Participants were instructed to search and count Gaussian blobs embedded in real scene images. While the researchers did not explicitly state why they used scenes for this task, it is important to note that low vision patients can improve performance for tasks that involve complex, real-world backgrounds (Janssen & Verghese, 2016; Vullings et al., 2022). Costela et al. (2019) had twenty - three patients with vision loss watch and describe 200 video clips of movies and television shows. After viewing each thirty second clip, participants were instructed to verbally describe the video. Description 

> 16

accuracy of each video was scored with a ”wisdom of the crowd” approach to assess the quantity of shared natural-language content among individual responses. Patients had significantly less shared words with other patients while controls had more shared words with other control participants, suggesting that vision loss negatively impacted overall scene perception (Costela et al., 2019). The effects of vision loss on scene perception with patients are supported by complementary work that tested sighted participants with CVL and PVL simulations for categorization (Larson & Loschky, 2009; Loschky et al., 2019) and visual search (Geringswald & Pollmann, 2015; McIlreavy et al., 2012; Nuthmann, 2014; Nuthmann & Canas-Bajo, 2022). 

Other work involving patients with different forms of vision loss have provided insight as to how humans process scenes. One study recruited participants with posterior cortical atrophy, a condition associated with Balint’s syndrome that includes symptoms of visual and cognitive impairment (Shakespeare et al., 2013). The participants completed three experiments: (1) scene gist categorization, (2) verbal scene descriptions, and (3) eye tracking when viewing scenes. Results showed that patients made significantly more errors and had longer response times compared to controls. Patient descriptions matched 40 percent of items from control participants. Patients also made more errors when reporting object identities or scene background settings. Eye tracking recordings show that patients with posterior cortical atrophy show no differences in fixation durations or saccade amplitudes compared to controls, differing from previous recordings with ARMD and RP patients (Shakespeare et al., 2013; Titchener et al., 2019; Vullings et al., 2022). A different 

> 17

study recruited patients with glaucoma. Patients had their visual fields and acuities assessed before performing detection and categorization tasks for scenes and faces of reduced contrast. Visual field analysis allowed researchers to separate patients into groups based on the presence of a central field defect. Acuity measurements revealed no differences between patients and controls, however, glaucoma patients made more errors for both scenes and faces compared to controls. Patients were much worse (had lower sensitivities) at scene categorization. Compared to glaucoma patients without central visual field defects, patients with central visual field defects exhibited the lowest sensitivities for categorizing scenes (Roux-Sibilon et al., 2018). 

Some studies that tested patients or sighted individuals with CVL or PVL simulations used scenes for categorization tasks (Larson & Loschky, 2009; Loschky et al., 2019; Peyrin et al., 2017; Thibaut et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2010). While this is useful for predicting effects of low vision, scene categorization assumes a specific hierarchy for scene processing: superordinate (i.e. fruit) , basic (i.e. apple), and subordinate (Granny Smith apple) levels (Fei-Fei et al., 2007). The level of explicit categorization can bias visual processing for features related to the target classes (Greene et al., 2015; Kadar & Ben-Shahar, 2012). Scenes in the real-world, especially those related to human behavior, typically contain other people performing a specific goal. While a person could be characterized as another object in a scene, there are sources of meaning found within the relationships and actions between different people and objects in the scene. Humans (and animals) can perceive and identify objects and actions very quickly, including the ability to rapidly infer the 

> 18

thoughts, emotions, and next actions of people (and other animals) in the scene (Boch et al., 2024; Greene et al., 2015; Lewicki et al., 2014). Based on the work from Fei-Fei et al. (2007) and Greene et al. (2015), for the purpose of the studies in this dissertation we define scene understanding as using social cues to infer relationships and actions between objects in an environment through perceptual processing. 

1.6 Scene Perception with Prosthetic Vision 

To date, there is no previous work evaluating how prosthetic vision affects scene perception. Tests for patients with prostheses rely on stimuli that are easier to recognize as a phosphene image. Real-world scenes have to be filtered by prosthetic devices in order to produce a clear image to the user. 

1.7 Organization of Dissertation 

In order to address these gaps in the literature, two experiments will be designed and tested using gaze - contingent visual display simulations. The first experiment will test the effects of simulated vision loss on rapid scene understanding, specifically comparing the effects of ARMD and RP (central vision loss and peripheral vision loss respectively) on the same naturalistic task. The second (two part) experiment will involve simulating prosthetic vision to understand how prosthetic vision affects scene understanding. Field of view and resolution will be tested to determine which properties contribute to scene perception. As visual prosthesis patients perform better with training, we test participants over 12 sessions to examine potential learning effects. 

> 19

This work will allow for measurable predictions on the impact of low and prosthetic vision on scene understanding and compensatory eye movement behaviors. Notably, all experiments will use the same low latency gaze - contingency system that will 1) allow for direct comparison between conditions and 2)update with a minimally perceived spatio-temporal lag. To predict performance of next generation prostheses, a new device utilizing prosthetic central vision in combination with natural peripheral vision will be simulated. 

> 20

II. Distinct Roles of Central and Peripheral Vision in Rapid Scene Understanding 

2.1 Introduction 

Chronic vision loss alters both perceptual processing and eye movement behavior, yet its impact on real-world scene understanding remains poorly understood. Two leading causes of progressive blindness (age-related macular degeneration and retinitis pigmentosa) produce bilateral scotomas that impair vision either centrally (CVL) or peripherally (PVL) (Shintani et al., 2009; Verghese et al., 2021). These conditions disrupt the typical mapping between visual input and retinal location, often leading to altered gaze strategies (Guadron, Titchener, Abbott, Ayton, van Opstal, et al., 2023; Janssen & Verghese, 2016; Legge & Chung, 2016; Seiple et al., 2013; Vullings et al., 2022). Previous studies have assessed the perceptual consequences of low vision using psychophysical tasks such as reading, face identification, and visual search (Geringswald & Pollmann, 2015; McIlreavy et al., 2012; Vice et al., 2022). Others have examined scene categorization (or ``gist'') using real-world images for patients with CVL or PVL (Peyrin et al., 2017; Thibaut et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2010). Yet these tasks capture only coarse semantic judgments and fail to reveal how vision loss affects higher-level understanding of real-world content. Richer scene interpretation, such as describing social interactions, requires extracting object relationships, context, and meaning beyond simple identification (Greene et al., 2015). Only a handful of studies have approached this question directly. 

> 21

Costela and colleagues found that patients with CVL gave less consistent verbal descriptions of dynamic scenes than sighted controls, suggesting degraded scene understanding (Costela et al., 2019). However, their study lacked eye-tracking, limiting insight into how visual sampling may have contributed. More generally, the link between gaze behavior and semantic scene interpretation in vision loss remains unclear. Gaze-contingent displays offer a powerful tool to simulate central or peripheral vision loss in a rapid and controlled manner (Kasowski et al., 2023). These paradigms preserve naturalistic viewing while selectively removing information from specific retinal regions. Simulations of CVL have been shown to affect face perception, reading, and oculomotor strategies (Tsank & Eckstein, 2017; Vice et al., 2022; Yu & Kwon, 2023), with consistent findings of increased saccade amplitude and delayed search performance (McIlreavy et al., 2012; Nuthmann, 2014). However, no prior study has applied these methods to open-ended scene understanding tasks or directly contrasted the effects of central and peripheral loss on semantic interpretation. To fill this gap, we combined biologically plausible gaze-contingent scotoma simulations with a rapid scene description task involving real-world images. Participants viewed scenes for one or three saccades under simulated CVL, PVL, or control conditions, and were asked to describe the scene content. Eye movements were recorded throughout, allowing us to test how visual sampling, fixation patterns, and semantic understanding are affected by different types of visual field loss. Our approach bridges the gap between low-level gaze metrics and high-level scene 

> 22

comprehension, offering new insights into how central and peripheral vision support everyday perception. 

2.2 Methods 

2.2.1 Participants We recruited 32 undergraduate students (5 male, 27 female, mean age of 19.88 years old). Participants were recruited from the Psychological and Brain Sciences Department at the University of California, Santa Barbara and completed the study for course credit. All participants provided informed consent. Experimental protocols were approved in accordance with the \ac{IRB} of the University of California, Santa Barbara. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. None of them reported having any known visual impairments. Any potential subject that could not pass the initial calibration test did not advance to the first trial and was excluded from the experiment. 2.2.2 Apparatus Python was used to program and run the experiment with scripts developed in-house. We specifically used PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) to present visual stimuli and control the eye tracker. The monitor used was an Alienware AW2524H monitor with 1280 × 1024 pixel resolution (31.3 × 24.8°) and a refresh speed of 480 Hz. The experiment was run on a Windows PC with an AMD Ryzen 7 3700X Processor (3.60 GHz). Participants were seated 68.6 cm away from the monitor with a headrest and chair to minimize head movements. Participants’ eyes were tracked monocularly using a SR Research Eyelink 1000 plus Tower Mount (SR Research ltd., Ontario, Canada) eye tracker. If 

> 23

calibration was unsuccessful with the right eye for whatever reason, we recorded from the left eye for that participant for the entirety of the experiment. A velocity threshold of 30° s −1 and acceleration threshold of 9500° s −2 was used to detect saccade events. The sampling rate for the eye tracker was 2000 Hz. Participants performed nine - point calibration before each block. If two or more broken fixations occurred during the forced fixation portion of each trial, participants were re -calibrated. 2.2.3 Stimuli Participants completed a rapid scene understanding task. Each image was a real-world scene scaled to 881.2 ± 61.7 × 600 pixels (21.8 × 14.7°). A total of 120 real-world scenes were used: ● “Social interaction” scenes: Half of the scenes were from a novel dataset of photos collected at the University of California, Santa Barbara. In this dataset, a premise for each scene was generated based on one or more actors interacting with one or more objects or people. Photographs of people acting as characters for these roles were taken to generate a dataset of social interaction photos. These scenes could also contain actors in the background. Example “social interaction” scenes are shown in the top row of Figure 1.

Figure 1: Representative images from the two scene categories used in the study. The top row shows social interaction scenes characterized by human presence and observable social behavior. The bottom row includes neutral scenes from the MS-COCO dataset, containing inanimate objects or animals without overt human interaction. ● “Neutral” scenes: The other half of the scenes were pseudo-randomly selected from the publicly available Microsoft Common Objects in Context (MSCOCO) image data set (Lin et al., 2014) used for machine learning and object recognition tasks. While half of the MSCOCO images contained at least one person ( 𝑛 = 30), others only contained empty rooms or animals. Importantly, the MSCOCO dataset was specifically designed for benchmarking computer vision model performance for object recognition. The bottom row of Figure 1 shows example “neutral” scenes. 

To explore the effects of low vision viewing conditions on scene understanding, participants were assigned to one of three conditions: none (control, 

𝑛 = 10), PVL ( 𝑛 = 11), and CVL ( 𝑛 = 11). One participant from the control group was unable to finish the study so they were excluded from the dataset. Participants 

> 25

viewed every scene in their assigned condition (e.g. between - subjects design). Participants were not aware of the experimental hypotheses and were not explicitly told the details of their viewing condition. 

To simulate PVL, concentric blur was applied to the image leaving a clear window with a diameter of 10°. While previous simulations have used a gray mask (Vice et al., 2022; Yu & Kwon, 2023), we used Gaussian blur from OpenCV (Bradski, 2000) for the simulated scotomas. This is because previous work with patients has shown that they are not always aware of the presence or location of their scotoma (Fletcher et al., 2012; Hartong et al., 2006; Peli et al., 2023). A solid filled mask has sharper edges that are more salient against a blank background, while Gaussian blur can make it more difficult for participants to detect the edges of the scotoma layered on a real-world scene. For CVL, an inner circular patch was blurred with the same Gaussian blur used for PVL. The size of the central scotoma matched the size of the clear window for the PVL condition (10°). This size was based on previous work simulating CVL for a visual search task (Kwon et al., 2013). Figure 2 shows an example scene of all three viewing conditions.

The display updated based on real-time recordings from the eye tracker to make the PVL and CVL simulations gaze-contingent. Before each trial, the stimulus was processed with the scotoma filtered at different locations of the image by subsampling every 40 pixels (1°) of the scene in order to present the simulation with minimal lag. Once the scene appeared, the center of the clear window or central scotoma appeared on the screen at the participants current fixation location and moved as participants made eye movements. The average delay between the eye tracker and the experiment monitor was 6.89 ± 1.21 ms (see Figure S1). 2.2.4 Procedure 2.2.4.1 Scene Presentation An overview of the experiment can be seen in Figure 3. The experiment was broken up into 12 blocks with 10 trials each, resulting in 120 trials. Before the experiment, scenes were randomly assigned to each block. While every participant had the same block sequence, the order of scenes within the block was randomized for each participant. The experiment was programmed to close at the end of each 

> 27

block. Participants were allowed to take as many breaks as they requested throughout the experiment. Experimental sessions were one to two hours in length and took place over two or more days. Figure 3: Overview of the experimental procedure. Each trial began with a central fixation cross. Participants ( 𝑛 = 32) viewed a natural scene under one of three simulated viewing conditions: unimpaired, peripheral vision loss (PVL), or central vision loss (CVL). Depending on the trial, participants were allowed either one or three saccades before the scene disappeared (randomized). They were then prompted to describe what they saw. No feedback was given. The same set of scenes was used across conditions and saccade limits, with presentation order counterbalanced across participants. Participants completed a rapid scene understanding task viewing all stimuli in their assigned simulation condition. After successful calibration, participants were shown a fixation cross in the middle of the screen. To start the trial, participants had to press the ‘space’ key while looking at the fixation cross for a random amount of time selected from a uniform distribution between 250 and 750 ms. If the participant 

> 28

moved their eyes away from the fixation cross for any reason, a “broken fixation” message would appear. Participants were re-calibrated after frequent broken fixations. Participant data was automatically saved after each trial. If the participant had to take a break or re-calibrate between trials, they would exit the program. Upon restarting, they would re-calibrate and continue with the next trial in sequence. If the participant fixated the central cross successfully (250 to 750 ms), the scene would appear. The amount of time for the stimulus presentation was dependent on the number of saccades made by the participant while viewing the scene. Before the experiment, half of the scenes were randomly assigned to allow for one saccade or three saccades. If a scene was assigned to allow for one saccade, upon stimulus onset, participants could make one saccade starting from the initial central fixation upon scene onset to their second fixation. If a scene was assigned to allow for three saccades, participants could make four fixations (initial central fixation at scene onset until completion of the fourth fixation). The simulated scotoma would update based on the participant’s current fixation location. Once the saccade limit was reached, upon the start of the next saccade, the scene disappeared and a gray screen was shown. If the saccade limit was not reached, the total maximum scene presentation time was 10 s. This fast presentation for scene perception is referred to as “rapid scene understanding”. 2.2.4.2 Response After the scene disappeared, participants were instructed to type a description of the scene in English. There was no strict length limit to their response but participants were encouraged to keep their descriptions shorter than four sentences. 

> 29

Text would appear on the screen as participants typed. No other feedback was provided about the quality of their descriptions. Verbal instructions for the scene description were given at the beginning of the experiment. The following instructions were presented on screen at the beginning of the experiment and every block: 1.  Double check descriptions for errors before submitting. 2.  Use complete sentences only. No one word sentences. 3.  Do not use proper nouns or names. 4.  Gender and pronouns can be used. 5.  Start your description with “There was a...” 6.  Only describe what you saw. Do not put “unclear” or “could not see it”. 2.2.5 Metrics 2.2.5.1 Scene Descriptions The semantic similarity between a ground-truth description of the scene and each participant response was computed as follows: ● Generating ground truth descriptions of each scene: To generate ground truth descriptions of each scene, a different group of five participants (5 female, mean age of 20.2 years old) were given the same scene task with unlimited viewing time and no simulated impairment. This provided five sets of ground truth descriptions to be used to evaluate the semantic similarity of responses from the rapid scene understanding task. To evaluate the upper limits of the ground truth descriptions, a separate group of five participants (5 female, mean age of 19.8 years old) compared four sets of ground truth

The fourth measure is saccade latency and was defined as the total amount of time between the scene appearing and the participant making a saccade. This was calculated for every trial and every recorded eye movement. If more than one saccade was allowed to view the scene, the latency was measured as the time between the end of the previous saccade and the beginning of the next saccade (i.e. fixation dwell time). 2.2.5.3 Fixation Heat Maps Analysis of participant eye movement behavior was based on five metrics to capture the spatial and temporal features of saccades. Distributions of participant fixation locations for a scene were measured by transforming fixation locations for every scene into separate heat maps for each viewing condition. To assess how fixations varied across viewing conditions (controls, PVL, and CVL) we compared fixation heat map correlations across viewing conditions to groups of different 

> 33

subjects in the control condition. Each heat map was generated by randomly sampling subjects ( 𝑛 = 4) into four groups for testing: one group of controls (“control comparability group”), a different group of controls to compare to the control comparability group, a group of PVL, and a group of CVL. All fixations recorded during the stimulus presentation were convolved with a Gaussian filter (39 × 39 pixels, or approximately 1 × 1°), providing a spatial representation of where participants fixated during each trial. Each heat map has a color map representing fixation density, where red indicates a high number of fixations relative to the rest of the map. Correlations between each control comparability group heat map and each viewing condition fixation heat map were computed for every scene. 2.2.5.4 Scene Segmentation and Frequency of Fixations to Objects Since we used real-world scenes containing people and objects, we wanted to understand if fixations to specific objects were affected by the viewing condition. The second measure based on eye movement behavior used annotations to determine how often participants fixated objects. One annotator (1 male, 19 years old) had unlimited time to outline faces and bodies of humans and animals as well as critical objects for all scenes. The annotations were created using Make Sense (Skalski, 2019) and saved into a .JSON file. Fixation locations separated by viewing condition and annotations were layered onto each scene, then the number of fixations that were located within an annotation were counted. Examples of annotated social interaction and neutral scenes are in Figure S7. Given that 61 of the 120 scenes presented (45 social interaction and 16 neutral) contained people located in the periphery (greater than 5 degrees visual 

> 34

angle) with respect to the fovea at the start of the trial) we classified each scene (ad hoc) with a binary label to determine if the effects of viewing condition on descriptions were affected by peripheral arrangements of people. Figure S4 shows an example scene classified as having a person located in the periphery upon stimulus onset. We repeated this labeling process for critical objects in the scenes. The critical object was defined as the most important object (or group of objects) needed to accurately describe the scene. Thirty-three of 120 scenes (21 social interaction, 12 neutral) were labeled as either including a critical object that was located in the periphery or a critical object that was located in the center of the scene. 2.2.6 Statistical Analyses 2.2.6.1 Description Ratings A linear mixed model lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) was used to assess the variance in human description ratings, including potential interactions between viewing condition (none, PVL, CVL), scene type (social interaction or neutral), and number of saccades allowed (one or three). Participants’ unique identifiers were included as a random factor to account for variability in semantic similarity across subjects. Post hoc comparisons were performed using Šidák correction to test for pairwise differences between conditions. 2.2.6.2 Analysis of Eye Movement Metrics For each trial, participants’ first saccade amplitude and first saccade latency were entered into an 𝐹 -test to assess whether these basic eye movement metrics varied across viewing conditions. 

> 35

2.2.6.3 Fixation Heat Map Similarity To assess how fixations varied across viewing conditions, fixation heat maps were generated for each group of subjects. Participants were randomly assigned to groups of four from each viewing condition: control, PVL, CVL, and a separate “control comparability group” composed of different control participants. Fixation locations were convolved with a Gaussian filter to produce a heat map for each scene and group. For each iteration, we computed the correlation between the heat map of an experimental group and the control comparability group. This procedure was repeated 100 times per scene, and average correlation scores were used in a linear mixed model to test whether heat map similarity was influenced by viewing condition, scene type, or number of saccades allowed. Scene ID was included as a random factor to account for variability due to specific scene content. Multiple comparisons were corrected using the Šidák method. A secondary analysis tested whether heat map similarity differed based on whether people or critical objects were located in the periphery. 2.2.6.4 Fixations to Annotated Objects The number of fixations to annotated humans and critical objects was computed per scene and viewing condition. A linear mixed model was used to test whether the number of object-directed fixations varied as a function of viewing condition, scene type, or number of saccades allowed. Scene ID was included as a random factor. Post-hoc Šidák-corrected comparisons were performed across conditions, and object arrangement (e.g., peripheral layout) was included as an additional binary predictor.
