2.4 Discussion 

This study demonstrates that simulated vision loss (both central and peripheral) impairs rapid scene understanding and alters early eye movement behavior in complex, naturalistic environments. By combining gaze-contingent visual impairment with human-rated scene descriptions, we show that the type of vision 

> 50

loss produces distinct effects: CVL primarily disrupted where participants looked, while PVL strongly impacted their understanding of the scene. Importantly, comprehension suffered most in social scenes, where describing meaningful interactions requires integration of multiple scene elements. These findings suggest that rapid scene understanding relies on both foveal detail and peripheral context, and that different forms of visual impairment disrupt this process in complementary ways. Our results extend prior work on scene categorization and simulated low vision (Loschky et al., 2019; Trouilloud et al., 2020) by using more ecologically valid stimuli and tasks. Descriptions from PVL and CVL participants were rated worse than controls, particularly for social interaction scenes (Fig. 4). This replicates and expands on prior evidence that peripheral vision supports rapid gist extraction (Larson & Loschky, 2009; Thibaut et al., 2016), and suggests that central vision is critical for resolving the social and semantic detail required to describe interactions. Notably, the neutral scenes (which often contained isolated objects or passive humans) produced smaller differences, likely because accurate description required only recognition rather than interpretation. Simulated vision loss also disrupted fixation behavior. CVL observers made larger first saccades (Fig. 5A) and had lower fixation heat map similarity to controls across all conditions (Fig. 6B–C). This contrasts with prior studies reporting smaller saccades in CVL patients with binocular scotoma during visual search (Vullings et al., 2022), or adaptive reductions in saccade range with training in simulations (Kwon et al., 2013; Vice et al., 2022). Our results suggest that under time pressure 

> 51

and without training, participants with central scotomas adopt a compensatory strategy of quickly fixating peripheral regions to avoid the blind spot. That PVL saccade amplitudes were indistinguishable from controls further supports the idea that CVL imposes stronger constraints on initial orienting. Heat map similarity to controls did not predict description quality, even among control participants (Fig.8A), suggesting that meaningful scene understanding depends not on looking in the same place, but on extracting the right information. Supporting this, fixations to annotated humans and critical objects were consistently linked to higher-rated descriptions across all groups (Fig.8B), underscoring the importance of semantically informative fixations—particularly in social scenes. Both PVL and CVL participants showed increased saccade latencies (Fig. 5B), consistent with prior studies of visual search and reading in patient populations and simulation paradigms (Ağaoğlu et al., 2022; Janssen & Verghese, 2016; Vice et al., 2022). Interestingly, CVL participants made faster and larger saccades than PVL participants, yet still produced higher-rated descriptions. One interpretation is that the central scotoma disrupted foveal detail but preserved access to scene context, whereas PVL observers struggled to localize targets and integrate spatial relationships due to a lack of peripheral preview. Supporting this view, saccade amplitude and latency were positively correlated in scenes with humans in the periphery (Fig. S8), particularly for CVL participants, suggesting that increased uncertainty delayed planning and triggered larger compensatory eye movements. Taken together, our findings suggest that peripheral vision supports rapid orienting and context estimation, while central vision provides access to high-acuity 

> 52

details needed for interpretation. Both are necessary for functional scene understanding in the real world. Simulations provide an informative approximation of patient behavior, but future studies should replicate these findings in clinical populations. It remains an open question how much adaptation or training can mitigate the observed deficits with simulations (Ağaoğlu et al., 2022; McIlreavy et al., 2012; Nuthmann & Canas-Bajo, 2022; Vice et al., 2022), or how training gaze strategies can influence experience-dependent plasticity in patients with chronic vision loss (Janssen & Verghese, 2016). Longitudinal studies and eye movement–based interventions could reveal whether patients can learn to optimize gaze strategies under naturalistic conditions. This work also highlights the value of naturalistic tasks, such as scene description, in assessing functional vision. Traditional clinical metrics like acuity and contrast sensitivity may not account for impairments in real-world understanding. Integrating eye tracking and semantically rich tasks could yield more sensitive and ecologically valid tools for evaluating patient outcomes and device efficacy. Furthermore, future work should explore how dynamic stimuli and active tasks, such as activities of daily living interact with vision loss. Our findings also emphasize the unique role of social information (i.e., faces, interactions, and people) in driving both visual behavior and semantic understanding. Functional assessments that ignore these dimensions may underestimate the real-world impact of vision loss. Finally, while simulations are not a substitute for patient studies, they offer a safe and scalable way to prototype interventions and evaluate scene comprehension under controlled conditions. By anchoring behavioral performance in both gaze 

> 53

behavior and semantic interpretation, our findings help bridge the gap between sensory impairment and functional vision and point toward more ecologically valid tools for vision assessment and rehabilitation.

III. Real-World Scene Understanding with High Resolution Wide Field Simulated Retinal Prosthetic Vision 

3.1 Introduction 

The PRIMA subretinal prosthesis is a vision restoration device that is currently being used in a clinical trial with patients (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2022). Until researchers can develop a device with less artificial, easier to interpret vision, the sparse patient population, invasiveness of the surgical procedure, potential safety risks, and artificiality of currently available devices limit the promise of visual prostheses to restore vision (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Levy et al., 2023; Nadolskis et al., 2024; Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). One advantage of using simulations to understand perception with prosthetic vision is the ability to test multiple design iterations of currently available and future prosthetic devices simultaneously (Kasowski et al., 2023). Simulations can be used in studies by modeling cortical prostheses for cases when only the higher visual pathway is accessible (area V1 or higher, no functioning retina or optic nerve) (Niketeghad & Pouratian, 2019). Retinal prostheses, such as PRIMA, Argus II, and the Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal devices have been tested in hundreds of patients (compared to the relatively smaller population of cortical implant recipients) (Finn et al., 2020; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Karapanos et al., 2021; Muqit et al., 2023). Researchers have reported that patients with retinal devices can perceive light and have measurable improvements in visual acuity (letter, grating, or Landolt C) (Ayton et al., 2014; A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020), however these improvements are limited and vary from patient to patient, 

> 55

leading to device abandonment (Erickson-Davis & Korzybska, 2021; Pérez Fornos et al., 2012). Many patients still have no measurable acuity when the device is turned on, such as those with Argus II (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Rachitskaya et al., 2020). Retinal prostheses are also designed to target a specific patient group based on cause of blindness. PRIMA is designed for patients with CVL and the device’s electrodes act by replacing the damaged photoreceptors that target the underlying bipolar cells (Palanker et al., 2022). The bipolar cells remain intact for cases of age-related macular degeneration, which is a disease condition that leads to CVL. The location of the electrode array on the retina is also specific to the cause of blindness. For example, since age-related macular degeneration patients have vision loss in the center of their retina due to central scotomas, PRIMA is implanted in the foveal region at the subretinal layer (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2022). The epiretinal Argus II and Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal Retinal devices were designed for patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP aka PVL or ‘tunnel vision’), so these arrays were implanted in the visual periphery and targeted the retinal ganglion cell layer (A. C. Ho et al., 2015; Karapanos et al., 2021). By specifying a retinal implant design type and location, we can better relate the perceptual effects to the cause and retinal area of blindness. One study that tested patients implanted with PRIMA reported an increase in letter acuity for 29 out of 38 participants (Muqit 2025 ARVO abstract). Earlier studies show improvements in acuity with a smaller sample of PRIMA participants (n = 3) and report that patients were able to read letters, words, and signs with the device 

> 56

turned on (Muqit et al., 2023; Palanker et al., 2020, 2022). The best reported acuities with the PRIMA device turned on ranged from 20/460 - 20/550 (1.37 - 1.44 logMAR) or 43.3 ETDRS letters (correct-to-normal acuity would be 20/20 Snellen, 0 logMAR, or 70 ETDRS) (Elliot et al., 1995). While promising, the extent to which visual prosthesis can fully restore functional vision is not well understood. PRIMA is roughly 7 degrees visual angle in diameter (2 mm in width) which is larger than the human foveola (1 degree visual angle diameter) but smaller than the typical scotoma size associated with later stages of age-related macular degeneration (diameter of 8.6 degrees visual angle) resulting in a smaller than natural field of view that can be conveyed by the device (Fletcher et al., 2012; Palanker et al., 2022; Tuten & Harmening, 2021; Whittaker et al., 1988). Results with patients using PRIMA suggest that when the device is turned on, patients see a small, prosthetic-filled aperture surrounded by the scotoma, but their natural peripheral vision beyond the scotoma’s eccentricity is intact (Palanker et al., 2020, 2022). While a larger prosthetic device could contribute to better perception overall, previous work has been unable to answer this question due to small form factors for devices likely necessary to maximize surgery success and minimize safety risks for patients. The visual prosthetic device with the largest field of view due to stimulation coverage is the Second-Generation (44-Channel) Suprachoroidal Retinal device at 38 by 28° visual angle (Karapanos et al., 2021). The device design is based on an earlier prototype that was smaller in size (19.44 by 19.2° visual angle) and limited to 24 electrodes (Petoe et al., 2017). 

> 57

Each device has a set number of electrodes (sometimes referred to as channels or pixels) with a given width. The size and number of electrodes could also influence perceptual clarity from visual prostheses. PRIMA arrays contain 378 hexagonal electrodes that are 100 μm in width (for comparison, a fovea with 1 degree visual angle diameter is approximately 288 μm). Another reason why perception with visual prostheses is degraded is due to technological limitations in engineering electrodes at a small enough size to mimic individual photoreceptors. Human cone photoreceptors have widths of 1 - 1.2 μm and send signals to receptive fields of bipolar cells (Mustafi et al., 2009).
